National  Anthem  from  1958-1971,  Wallah  Zaman  Ya Selahy  by  famous  singer  Umm  Kulthum,  also
mirrors  this  language,  “Oh  what  the  enemy  shall see  from  you  (Egyptian  soldiers)  in the  fire of  the
battlefield”.49  Similar  declarations  of  Egyptian  soldiers,  implicitly  supported  by  Nasser,  “smash(ing)
the thorn  of  colonialism”  with  “the  title of revolutionary  victory  was  in every  free country”  are  made
in Al  Geal  El  Saeed.50  Indeed,  some  of  Nasser’s  actual  actions  did  help  minimise  the potential  for
immediate  defeat.  For  example,  he  ordered  the evacuation  of  Egyptian  troops  from  Sinai  after  the
Israeli attack  had  begun  in  anticipation  of  the  British  attack  on  the  Canal  after  witnessing  their air
attacks.51 This  would  help  ensure  the  invasion  wasn’t  a  swift victory  for  the British.  However,  this is a
minor  act in the  grand  scheme  of events,  especially  considering  Egypt  never  achieved  military  victory
and  instead  relied on  political  outrage  and  diplomatic  pressure.
Numerous  historians,  such  as  Steven  Cook,  assert that  itwas  the  United  States’  stance  against
the  war  that  ultimately  pushed  the  British  out  of Egyptian  domestic  affairs.52  This  is supported  by
documents  from  official  British  cabinet  meetings,  such  as  the meeting  where  they  discussed  their
declining  economic  position,  where  a  highlighted  reality  was  their  need  for  US  economic  assistance
and  their  inability  to obtain  it due  to  their actions  in the  Crisis.53  In  fact, the final  straw  was  when
Eisenhower  didn’t  support  Eden’s  pursuit  of a $1  billion loan  from  the International  Monetary  Fund.54
The  fact  that  the US  played  such  a  big  role in  the  crisis shows  that there  is a dissonance  between
propaganda  and  reality, where  propaganda  consistently  perpetuated  an  inaccurate  image  of Nasser  just
as the  man  who  nationalised  the  Suez  Canal,  but  also  as  the  man  who  successfully  ravaged  the
enemies’  armies  even  under  impossible  conditions.
The  concept  of victory  against  the  powerful  oppressors  after so  many  years  of struggle  was
overwhelming  to Egyptians.  Ahmed  describes  how  “despite  his shortcomings”,  the most  prominent
part  of Nasser’s  “legacy”  in his  memory  is how  he  led  Egypt  against  Britain,  “a  hugely  powerful
country”  and  “overcame”  them.”55  This  again  displays  an underlying  belief  that Nasser  was  the  cause
of  Egyptian  victory  over  the  British  and  French.  Furthermore,  Ahmed’s  words  reveal  how,  in
believing  Nasser  was  the  cause  of  victory,  Egyptians  finally  believed  their capabilities  could  be
expanded,  particularly  after decades  of  failure  to eliminate  repressive  colonialist  presence  in Egypt
with  previous  governments,  because  an  Egyptian  had  led  them  to victory  and  lived up  to  his words.
Mariam  also  comments  that in  winning  the war,  Nasser  had  achieved  “the  impossible”  56 and  how
“overjoyed”57  she  was  at that fact. To  Egyptians,  Nasser  did  not merely  win  the war,  he  revived  Egypt,
belief in Egypt’s  potential  and  pride  in Egyptian  national  identity.
Of  course,  Egyptians  weren’t  completely  ignorant  of the role  of American  opposition.  Mariam
acknowledges  that  the  American  helped  end  the  war.58  Yet,  the specific  diction  highlighted  above
perpetually  reveals  an  underlying  subconscious  belief  in an  exaggerated  view  of  Nasser’s  role.  For
example,  Mariam  discusses  how  through  achieving  victory  under  unfavourable  conditions,  Nasser
restored  “that sense  of hope”  that Egyptians  “could  be  more”.59

The  victory  in the  war  being  deemed  as Nasser’s  victory  was  more  significant  in legitimising
Nasser  than  even  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was.  The  nationalisation  highlighted  Nasser’s
courage  and  lack  of hesitance  to act towards  progress,  unlike  his predecessors.  Yet, as revealed  by the
above  comments,  his  ‘victory’  over  the  aggressors  solidifies  him  as  not  merely  courageous  but
substantively  capable  of  leading  Egypt  beyond  its colonial  past.  This  would  consequently  instil great,
potentially  blind,  trust in Nasser  as a  leader  and  his Arab  Nationalist  ideology  beyond  the Suez  Crisis
to mythological  levels, thereby  intensely.
Thus,  Nasser’s  effort  to  nationalise  the  Canal  was  a  bold  move  that  helped  propagate  his
persona  as  Egyptians  were  overjoyed  simply  to  observe  concrete  action  being  taken.  However,
Egypt’s  victory  in the  war  was  more  significant  as it provided  Nasser’s  words  with  tangible  results
previously  thought  unobtainable  and  promulgated  a new  sense  of  hope  throughout  Egypt  in the
country’s  potential,  cementing  Nasser’s  cult  of  personality  as the  much  stronger  and  more  effective
leader  in  the process.  Yet,  Egypt’s  victory  was  not  a result  of Nasser’s  actions.  Instead,  he  solidified
the idea  that they  were  through  propaganda.  Therefore,  propaganda  painting  Nasser  as the  cause  of
Egypt’s  victory  is what  cemented  his  cult  of personality  and  allowed  him  to become,  as  Anwar  El
Sadat  claimed,  an  “Egyptian  mythological  hero”.60

Costs  of War  and  Battling  the  Colonialists

As  is conventional  for  war-time  propaganda,  Nasser’s  propaganda  glorified  the  costs  of war  as
necessary  losses  to Egypt’s  liberation,  implying  that  propaganda  allowed  Nasser  to palliate  the  costs
of war.  An  example  of this  isin  ‘Sawt  Al  Arab’  (Voice  of  the Arabs),  a nationalistic  radio  program  run
by  the Egyptian  government  which  was  also  widely  popular  over  the  whole  Arab  world.61  Numerous
enthusiastic  speeches  calling  to  Egyptians  “to strike  out  against  the  aggressors”62  aired  frequently,
alongside  Nasser  himself  claiming  it to be  a duty  of the  people  “to  struggle  to get  the  enemy  out  of
their country”63  and  playing  nationalistic  songs.64  Mariam  claims  that in the  aftermath  of the  Crisis,
Egyptians  were  “overwhelmed  with  joy”.65  She  passionately  asserts  the  necessity  of  martyrs  and
glorifies  their deaths  because  “they  died  fighting  for  the freedom  of  their country”.66  Suffering  in war
is intertwined  with  a sense  of the  honour  and  vindication  of obtaining  freedom,  thereby  transforming
that suffering  into  a  source  of pride  in  of itself. Egypt  experienced  the  heaviest  losses  in  the war  on
every  front,  as  it took  place  entirely  on  Egyptian  soil  and  in  Egyptians  towns  that  were  destroyed,67
and  having  the  highest  number  of  casualties.68  Infrastructure  was  badly  damaged  during  the  war,
particularly  when  itcame  to transportation  like  railways,  roads  and  airports,69  a particularly  difficult
setback  for  a  nation  pushing  industrialisation.70  Egypt  opted  to  blockade  the  Canal,  causing  an

However,  this  feature  of  Nasser’s  propaganda  is merely  a  reflection  of  the  context  Egypt
faced.  Nasser  had  committed  a provocative  but  legal  action  in nationalising  the Suez  Canal.72  The  fact
that Eden  had  seen  this action  as a threat  and  was  determined  to destroy  Nasser  and  reassert  British
military  presence  in  the Canal  for it is evidence  that  he  was  an  aggressor  and  a real threat  to Egypt’s

the true  aggressor,  with  the British-French  request  for a  ceasefire  between  Egypt  and  Israel  being
intentionally  done  in  a  manner  that  would  weaken  Egypt’s  position  comparatively,  making  it
impossible  for Nasser  to  accept.74  Thus,  it was  Britain’s  own  actions  which  reinforced  the  popular
public  conception  that  it was  stilloperating  under  the apparatus  of an  oppressive  colonialist  state in
Egypt.  Ahmed  observes  how  “Britain  was  being  ridiculous”  in beginning  the  war  “just  because  we
nationalised  something  in  our  own  land”.75  Mariam  also  acknowledges  that “no  one  was  happy  their
country  was  being  invaded,  but  the people  were  ready  to fight”.76 This  notion  was  omnipresent  across
Egypt  and  instigated  a great  deal  of unified  action  amongst  civilians.  Civilians  were  given  guns  and
encouraged  to  fight  themselves,  resulting  in numerous  civilian  makeshift  troops.77  Samir  Ghanem,  a
member  of the  Egyptian  military  intelligence  at the  time,  claimed  “every  Egyptian  was  willing  to
sacrifice  himself  to  defend  his  country”.78  This  may  be  exaggeratory,  given  Ghanem’s  position,
however  these  claims  are  somewhat  supported  by  Mariam,  who  details  how  her brother  attempted  to
get personally  involved  in the  struggle  and  claims  “the  regular  people  were  fighting”,79  “when  faced
with  an  external  threat,  we  unified”.80  Common  cause  was  established  between  Nasser  and  his  people
through  the creation  of a  common  enemy.  The  destruction  of war  was  not  whitewashed,  but rather  the
responsibility  of that  destruction  was  rightly  allocated  to  the real aggressors  rather  than  Nasser,  which
in turn allowed  for that  destruction  to be a symbol  of the resilience  of Egyptian  nationalism.
Nasser’s  power  was  aided  by  the destruction  of  war  as  itallowed  him  to capitalise  on Britain
proving  themselves  to be  the  oppressive  colonialists  Egyptians  saw  them  as. As  with  the  case  of the
nationalisation  of the  Suez  Canal,  Egyptian  state-owned  media  did not  manufacture  the impact  of the
aggressors’  oppression.  Rather,  it constantly  perpetuated  narratives  of it and  capitalised  on  it to
amplify  the  nationwide  sense  of unified  resistance.  Nasser’s  actions  in  creating  civilian  troops  also
had  a  similar  effect.  Hence,  both  Nasser’s  actions  and  propaganda  capitalised  on  anti-colonialist
sentiment,  but  itwas  the actions  of Britain,  France  and  Israel,  both  in the Suez  Crisis  and  previously,
which  created  the foundation  of that sense  in the Egyptian  public  mind.

Conclusion

The  Suez  Crisis  greatly  elevated  Nasser’s  power.  Many  of  Nasser’s  actions  helped  him  maintain  his
power,  such  as the  shocking  defiance  and  strength  he  demonstrated  in nationalising  the Canal  and  his
strategic  decision-making  during  the war.  Often,  Egyptian  unity  with  Nasser  was  effectively  promoted
by  propaganda  surrounding  the  destruction  of  the  war,  but  it was  not  founded  on  itas  anti-Western

the nationalisation  of the  Canal  and  the  myth  of Nasser  as  the man  who  achieved  victory.  The  latter
most  majorly  contributed  to Nasser’s  power  as Egypt  had  failed  for  decades  to do  so,  making  such  a
victory  seem  ‘impossible’.  Thus,  Nasser  ‘achieving  victory’  mythologised  him  and  created  an
overwhelming  sense  of trust  not just  in his courage  but  also in  his infallibility.It also  restored  hope  in
the potential  for Egyptian  greatness  in the  future,  validating  and  popularising  Nasser’s  ideology  of
Arab  Nationalism.  Therefore,  the  presentation  of the  Suez  Crisis  was  more  significant  to Nasser’s
maintenance  of  power  than  Nasser’s  actions.
This  case  study  of Nasser  reveals  much  about  the machinations  of power  for authoritarians  in
post-colonial  states.  Even  after decolonisation,  the  lasting  influence  of Britain  maintained  a sense  of
oppression  in the  Egyptian  public  mind,  and  this  continued  to be  one  of the  most  salient  areas  of
political discontent.  What  was  most  pertinent,  however,  was  not  Nasser’s  real  demonstration  of his
capabilities  through  his  actions,  but  rather  the  perception  of  Nasser’s  ability  to  ‘beat  back’  the
colonisers.  Nasser’s  competency  was  not  a  prerequisite  to  his  popularity  but  was  sufficiently
compensated  by  the  perception  his propaganda  was  able  to promulgate.  On  Nasser,  Fouad  Ajami
comments  that  “the  calculus  of  achievements  and  errors  doesn’t  seem  to  apply  to  charismatic
leaders”.81  Whilst  not untrue,  itis essential  to understand  the context  under  which  this charisma  arose.
It was  not  merely  Nasser’s  charisma,  but  rather  his  strongman  appearance  before  what  Egyptians
believed  to be  an  impossible  enemy,  with  much  desperation  to  find  someone  willing  to fight  back
rather than  rely on  Britain’s  endorsement  to maintain  their  power.

Interview  1: Ahmed  (Egyptian  male.  Born:  1959)
1.  How  well  known  was  Hafez’s  Heyaket  Sha’b?
Everyone  was  singing  it,whether  old or young,  doorman  or university  graduate.  When  Abdel  Halim
was  singing  itone  time,  he was  begged  to repeat  itby  the audience  (instead  of moving  onto  the next
song). The  fact  that the song  is ineasy  Egyptian  Arabic,  compared  to Abdel  Halim’s  other  songs,  also
made  it easier to remember.

2.  How  did you/others  feel when  listening to it?
Itmakes  one  feel proud  and  appreciative  of what  these  people  (Nasser  and  his new  government)  have
achieved.

3.  With  what  happened  in the war  and  those  who  passed?
No, this song  was  more  so  todo  with  the fact that we  wanted  to do  something  to improve  our country.
Everyone  stood  against  us to prevent  us from  doing  it,yet  we  prevailed  and  achieved  it.‘Hekayet
Sha’b’  confirms  that fact, like we  say in the song,  ‘we  said  we’d  build  and we  did build  the High
Dam,  oh colonialists  we  built with  our hands  the High  Dam,  with  our  money,  with  the hands  of our
workers.’  It’s as ifyou’re  confronting  the  colonialists with  the fact of  our victory  over  them  despite
our size and  inferior position.

4.  What  did your  family  endure  under  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser?
My  uncle  Kamal  had  sent  Nasser  a letter warning  him  to ‘fear Allah’.  Nasser  had  just been  arresting
members  of the Muslim  Brotherhood  around  the time  and  my  uncle  had  heard  about  the torture they
endured.  This  letter reached  Nasser  the night  of his eldest daughter’s  wedding,  so  he put my  uncle
under  house  arrest. His  wife passed  away  during  that time. After  that the rest of my  family  was
watched  by the  government  closely. My  dad  lost his job and  was  imprisoned  for 3-4  weeks.  My  other
uncle also  was  for around  3 years.

5.  How  do  you personally  feel about  Nasser?
He’s a character  who  frustrates  me  very  deeply  because  he did  so many  things  that liberated  this
country  and  re-instilled pride  and belief  in our ability to prevail  (in Suez)  but he  also made  so many
mistakes  afterwards  that we  are stillpaying  the price  of.However,  overall,  despite  his flaws, I believe
inthe  legacy  he left behind.  Britain  was  being  ridiculous  in orchestrating  the war  just because  we
nationalized  something  in our own  land. They  simply  wanted  to maintain  their control  over  us in any
way,  shape  or form.  This  hugely  powerful  country  had  stood  against us  and  our development  with
nationalizing  the Canal  and  building  the High  Dam,  yet we  overcame  them  under  Nasser’s  rule and
managed  to push  them  down.  That  to me  is the more  prominent  part of his legacy,  despite  all his
shortcomings.

Interview  2: Mariam  (Egyptian  female.  Born:  1939)
6.  How  well  did ‘Hekayet  Sha’b’  reflect the  events at the  time?
Perfectly. Just perfectly.  That  was  the genius  of Abdel  Halim,  itwasn’t  just his voice  or the  music,  but
itwas  also the  topics he  would  pick.

7.  How  did Egyptians  react after hearing  the nationalisation  speech?
All of Egypt  was  jumping  with  joy. In every  house  you  would  find  people  dancing  and  cheering.  We
were  allextremely  happy  with  the nationalisation  of the Canal  since this was  a very  old  and sacred

Propagandaor Reality?

dream  for Egyptians.  I don’t  remember  the exact  numbers,  but Egypt  had lost so  many  in the digging
of the Canal,  so many  who  had  endured  poor  conditions  such  as no food  or water  and  terrible heat.

8.  Nasser  mentioned  something  along  those  lines in his speech.
Yes, but  thisis true. They  barely paid  them.  So  many  died.

9.  Was  no  one  afraid  ofthe  repercussions  of nationalizing  the Canal?
Itwould  pass. No  one really  thought  about  those  issues. It’s not the people  who  consider  these
technicalities, its Nasser.  He’s  the one  who’s  responsible  for them.  We  were  just extremely  jubilant.

10.  How  did people  feel during  the invasion?
Of course,  no  one  was  happy  that their country  was  being  invaded,  but the  people  were  ready  to fight
and do  the impossible.  I remember  my  brother, Fathy,  was  going  to go  fight himself,  but  of course  my
family  stopped  him.  The  people  wanted  to do something.  The  regular  people  were  fighting. Unlike
when  Denshawai  happened,  we  finally  had  an opportunity  to fight back.  Despite  allthis country’s
flaws, whenever  we  faced  an  external threat, the  whole  country  goes  in one  direction  (euphemism  in
Arabic  for unity).

11.  How  did people  feel in the aftermath  of the Crisis?
Everyone  was  just overwhelmed  with  joy.Nasser  finally returned  to us  what  was  rightfully  ours and
our independence.  We  needed  that sense  of hope  restored,  that we  were  strong  enough  and  could  be
more.

12.  Was  there  a sense  of loss over  those  who  passed?
Of course,  but  they died  fighting  for the freedom  of their country.  It reminded  everyone  of what  we
had suffered  at the hands  of the colonialists.

13.  How  did you  feel about  Nasser  afterwards?
Iknow  that the  Americans  and  Soviets  were  the ones  who  forced  the colonialists  to step down,  but  I
was  so proud  that an  Egyptian  could  achieve  this.Nasser  was  able to make  us  feel that hope  again.  I
was  proud  to call myself  Egyptian,  and  to call him  my  president.

14.  Do  you  think Nasser  was  a  better leader  than  the Wafd  government?
Yes. They  seemed  so paralyzed  and  polarized,  they  were  unable  to act in any direction  or  decide  on
anything.  Nasser  clearly didn’t  have  that issue. That  is why  we  sometimes  need  dictatorship.

Propaganda  or  Reality?  Reevaluating  the  Tripartite
Aggression  and  the  Dynamics  of  Post-Colonial  Power

Salma  Abuelatta

Abstract

By  1954,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser  had  successfully  consolidated  power  and
outmanoeuvred  internal  opposition.  After  Britain,  the  United  States  and  the
International  Bank  withdrew  their  offers  to  fund  the High  Aswan  Dam,  Nasser
resolved  to  nationalise  the British  and  French  owned  Suez  Canal  Company.  In the
ensuing  Suez  War,  despite  Egypt’s  military  defeat  at the  hands  of Britain,  France
and  Israel,  Nasser’s  power  and  popularity  were  amplified,  arguably  to  mythological
levels.  He  remains  a  monumental  figure  of  pride  to many  in contemporary  Egypt,
particularly  due  to the  Suez  Crisis.  Whether  this isdue  to the  success  of  his actions
and  policies,  or  charisma  and  propaganda,  remains  unclear.  Through  the  case  study
of  Nasser,  this paper  aims  to  identify  patterns  of how  dictators  in  quasi-colonised
and  post-colonial  states  construct  narratives  against  and  manipulate  the unpopularity
of  oppressive  colonialist  nations  to fortify their  own  power.  This  essay  argues  that
although  Nasser  did  help  eliminate  the  remnants  of  British  and  French  colonial
presence  in  Egypt,  his  successes  in  aggrandising  certain  aspects  of  the  Crisis
through  propaganda  was  more  significant  to cultivating  his mythological  status  and
power.
Keywords:  Post-colonial  states, Egypt,  Suez  Crisis,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser,  Middle
Eastern  History,  British  Foreign  Policy,  Collapse  of the British  Empire,  Suez  Canal

Introduction

By  1954,  Gamal  Abdel  Nasser  had  successfully  consolidated  power  and  outmanoeuvred  internal
opposition.1  In July  1956,  Britain,  the  United  States  and  the  International  Bank  withdrew  their offers
to fund  Nasser’s  project,  the  High  Aswan  Dam,  citing  Egypt’s  bankruptcy,  although  the  true reason
was  Nasser’s  flirtations with  the East  during  the  Cold  War.2  In retaliation,  Nasser  set  his sights  on
nationalising  the  Suez  Canal  Company,  which  he  estimated  could  potentially  cover  the  costs  of the
Dam  alone,  and  he  did  so  on July  26,  1956.3  British  and  French  ownership  of Suez  Canal  Company

seen  in  how  when  the  1967  Six-Day  War  concluded  in a  humiliating  defeat  for Egypt,  and  Nasser
resolved  to  resign  as  a  result, there  were  protests  on  the streets  calling  for  his  return.7 He  remains  a
monumental  figure  of  pride  to many  in contemporary  Egypt,  especially  due  to the  Crisis.8  Whether
this is due  to the  success  of his  actions  and  policies,  or  charisma  and  propaganda  remains  unclear.  It is
worth  re-evaluating  how  dictators  in  quasi-colonised  countries  use  rhetoric  against  colonialist
aggressor  nations  to fortify their  power  to the  extent  of creating  such  loyalty.9
Outside  of  secondary  literature,  this essay  will  draw  upon  primary  research  in  the form  of
interviews  conducted  with  middle-class  Egyptians,  Mariam  who  was  17  years  old at  the time  of the
Suez  Crisis,  and  Ahmed,  who  was  born  in 1959  and  grew  up  in the  ensuing  aftermath.  Their  names
have  been  changed  for  anonymity.  This  is supplemented  by  other  external  accounts,  popular  music,
the British  cabinet’s  meeting  minutes,  and  Nasser’s  speeches  to examine  the impact  of propaganda  on
public  opinion.  This  paper  is split  into themed  sections  oriented  around  different  aspects  of the  Crisis
and  the  nationalisation  of  the  Suez  Canal  that  helped  Nasser  maintain  his  power.  Each  section
examines  whether  it was  presentation,  such  as  propaganda  and  Nasser’s  charisma,  or reality,  as  in
Nasser’s  concrete  actions,  policies,  and  results,  that aided  Nasser’s  maintenance  of power.  I argue  that
although  Nasser  did  help  eliminate  the  remnants  of  colonial  presence  in  Egypt,  his  success  in
aggrandising  certain  aspects  of the  Crisis through  propaganda  was  more  significant  to his  maintenance
of power.

Funds  and  The  High  Aswan  Dam

In his initial announcement  of the nationalisation  of  the Canal  on  July  26 1956,  Nasser  made  repeating
reference  to one  argument  for  nationalising  the  Canal:  itsenormous  financial  potential,  particularly  to

detrimental  annual  flooding  from  the  Nile,  thus  increasing  farmland  by  20-30%,10  as  well  as  store
additional  water  in  the Lake  Nasser  reservoir  for irrigation.11  However,  the Dam  was  barely  funded  by
Canal  revenue.12  Instead,  Egypt  primarily  used  Soviet  loans  acquired  in  1958.13  Therefore,  the  Dam

Yet,  the  High  Dam  seems  to  have  been  eternalised  in the collective  Egyptian  mind  as being  a

popular  celebrities,  making  his  music  greatly  influential.15  Therefore,  his  song  is  useful  to
understanding  public  opinion.  The  song  details  how  Egyptians  built  the Dam  “with  our own  money”16
(referencing  Canal  proceeds),  despite  the  fact itwas  released  after the  Soviets  agreed  to aid in funding
the Dam,  thus  linking  the  two  together  more  than  was  reality. 17 Moreover,  there  ismuch  evidence  that
these  messages  effectively  impacted  Egyptian  audiences.  The  song  is laid  out  as a simple  emotive
narrative  and  uses  simpler  language,18  thereby  making  it more  memorable  and  accessible  to allclasses
of Egyptians,  particularly  because  Egypt  had  an  illiteracy  rate of  77.2%  in 1947.  19 Historian  Joel
Gordon  comments  that  all the  “Wataniya”  songs  generally  from  this time  had  a similar  joyous
atmosphere  and  were  made  to  be  accessible  to the  lower  class.20  Ahmed  claims  that everyone  was
listening  to (Hafez’s  song).21  Indeed,  Ahmed  even  directly  parallels  claims  made  in the  song,  with
Hafez’s  song  stating  “nationalisation  irritated the  colonialists,  why  should  we  be able  to  restore  our
glory?”22  and  Ahmed  noting  “we  wanted  to  improve  our  country,  everyone  stood  against  us”.23
Mariam  also  adds  that the  song  ‘perfectly’  embodied  the Crisis.24 This  reveals  how  the song  was  able
to directly impact  Egyptians’  opinions.
This  combination  of  presenting  the Dam  as a symbol  of  the struggle  against  colonialism  and  a
symbol  of  Egypt’s  advancement  helped  popularise  the  belief  that  ‘the  colonialists’  were  not  just
attempting  to maintain  their power,  but  were  purposefully  aiming  to undermine  Egypt’s  progress  and
‘return  to greatness’  by  refusing  to  finance  it, and  indeed,  Ahmed  refers  to the invasion  as an  attempt
to thwart  Egypt’s  progress.25  This  garnered  support  for Nasser,  because  he  was  the  man  known  for
building  the  Dam  and  fighting  colonialist  oppression  by defiantly  nationalizing  the Canal.  This  can  be
seen  in the  popular  nationalist  song  Al Geal  El Saeed,  released  in 1960  by  Mohammed  Abdel  Wahab,
which  concludes  with  references  to how  Egyptians  “Build  with  you  (Nasser)”.26
The  Dam  was  an  important  factor  in bolstering  Nasser’s  maintenance  of power  as it served  as
a symbol  of Egypt’s  progress.  However,  itwasn’t  a consequence  of the  nationalisation  of the  Canal.
The  way  the  Dam  was  presented  in relation  to the  Crisis  in popular  media,  helped  engineer  the
popular  perception  that the  Dam,  this symbol  of progress’,  existence  was  intimately  dependent  on  the
Suez  Crisis,  thus  making  Egypt’s  advancement  in general  seem  dependent  on  the  Crisis. Therefore,
the presentation  of  the Crisis  was  more  significant  to Nasser’s  maintenance  of power  in  the case  of the
High  Aswan  Dam.

Cementing  Nasser’s  Cult  of Personality

Nationalising  the  Canal
Through  the  act of  nationalising  the  Canal,  Nasser  was  able  to validate  his regime’s  anti-colonialist
rhetoric  and  affirm  his  persona  as the only  man  who  sticks to his word  and  is defiant  in the face  of the
colonialists, thus  enhancing  his power.
The  weakness  of the  previous  government  in its handling  of  British control  over  Egypt  was  a
key  factor  to its downfall.  When  King  Farouk  refused  to appoint  a Wafd  government  at the behest  of
the British  in  1942,  tanks  were  positioned  outside  his  palace  in a show  of force,  forcing  Farouk  to
concede.  27Cook  claims  this  incident  significantly  discredited  both  the  parliamentary  system  and  the
monarchy.28  Indeed,  this incident  showcased  the  government’s  subservience  to  the British  as  well  as
highlighting  the inability  of Farouk  and  parliamentary  parties  to be an  effective  united  front  in the face
of British  interference.  Considering  how  important  abolishing  British  presence  was  to Egyptians,  the
government’s  inability to  do  so made  them  seem  inept  and  inadequate.  Therefore,  Nasser  standing  up
to the British  so  openly  and  seemingly  fearlessly  for Egyptian  interests contrasted  with  such  incidents
where  fear  of  the  British  seemed  to  dictate  Egyptian  leaders’  actions.  Mariam  asserts  “they  (the
previous  government)  were  unable  to act…  Nasser  clearly  didn’t  have  that  issue”.29
Due  to  this context,  some  historians,  such  as  Joel  Gordon,  argue  that  no  propaganda  could
save  the  regime  -  only  action.30  Certainly,  Nasser  was  initially  in a  tumultuous  and  contentious
position,  as  highlighted  by  the  March  Crisis  of 1954,  where  Nasser  and  his  Command  Council
Revolutionary  (CCR)  had  battled  a  beloved  military  figure,  Mohammed  Naguib,  for  the position  of
Egypt’s  leader.  There  had  even  been  protests  demanding  Nasser’s  head  and  200  military  officers
protested  in  favor  of Naguib.31  Yet,  by  the point  of  the Suez  Crisis,  Nasser’s  power  and  persona  was
arguably  widely  consolidated.  In the  Manshiya  incident  of October  26, 1954,  Mahmoud  Abdel  Latif, a
member  of  the  Muslim  Brotherhood,32  failed  to assassinate  Nasser  while  he was  giving  a speech  in
Manshiya  Square.  33 Nasser  capitalised  on  the  opportunity,  giving  his iconic  “Each  of  you  is Gamal
Abdel  Nasser”  speech  which  turned  public  opinion  strongly  in his favour,  34 consequentially  enabling
his crackdown  of  the  Muslim  Brotherhood  with  mass  arrests.35 In  fact, civilians  themselves  across
Cairo  set  fire to Muslim  Brotherhood  headquarters.36  Thus,  Nasser  had  already  acquired  a decently
stable level  of power  and  public  support  by  the  time  of the  Suez  Crisis, and  he  managed  to do  so by
using  opportunistic  propaganda,  suggesting  that  it is entirely  within  the  realm  of  possibility  that the
popularity  surrounding  his  decision  to nationalise  the  Canal  was  more  majorly  manufactured  by
propaganda  than  the act in of  itself.
Indeed,  Nasser’s  speech  announcing  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was  extremely
sensational.  He  gave  it in Manshiya  Square,  recalling  to Egyptian’s  his previous  inflammatory  speech
in the Manshiya  Incident  and  hence  evoking  a stronger  sense  of support.  Beyond  this,the  speech  was

Still, whilst  Nasser’s  propaganda  may  have  amplified  the  potency  of  his  actions,  there  is
reason  to believe  that  the desire  to stand  up  to colonialist  oppression  did not  originate  with  Nasser’s
speech.40  A  minister  in Nasser’s  cabinet,  Sami  Sharaf,  claimed  he felt “internally  proud”  when  Nasser
firstsuggested  nationalising  the Suez  Canal  Company  to him  in private,  prior  to  the speech.41  While
Sharaf  may  be  embellishing,  Mariam  adds  further  credence  by  stating  that  the reason  the  Egyptian
public  was  overjoyed  by  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was  because  itwas  an  ancient,  pre-existing
dream  Nasser  had  managed  to  fulfil,not  one  he  pioneered.42  While  the ‘120,000’  figure  iscontentious,
there  are  numerous  other  examples  of  colonialist  oppression  that  would  make  Egyptians  desire  a
general  complete  removal  of  British  presence.  A  notable  example  is the  Denshawai  Incident  of  1906,
where  a  confrontation  between  British  soldiers  and  Egyptian  villagers  led  to mass  unjust  executions
and  sentences  of  hard  labour.43  The  incident  lived  on  in the  Egyptian  memory,  as  evidenced  by
Mariams  joy  that  Egyptians  could  fight  back  during  the  war  “unlike  Denshawai”44  and  casual
references  to it by  famous  journalists  such  as Muhammed  Heikal.45
Nasser’s  speech  was  effective  in  amplifying  public  support,  and  iteven  exaggerated  certain
details  to ensure  enough  outrage  at  the  Suez  Canal’s  colonial  past.  Yet,  Nasser’s  actual  action  was
capitalising  on,  and  not  pioneering,  pre-existing  strongly  established  Egyptian  desires  to remove  the
British  entirely.  Thus,  Nasser’s  actions  in nationalising  the Canal,  more  significantly  than  propaganda,
solidified  his  strength  of  character  and  cemented  him  as  an  improvement  upon  ‘the  old  order’  of
government  and  politicians.

powerful  militaries.

the thorn  of  colonialism”  with  “the  title of revolutionary  victory  was  in every  free country”  are  made

immediate  defeat.  For  example,  he  ordered  the evacuation  of  Egyptian  troops  from  Sinai  after  the

attacks.51 This  would  help  ensure  the  invasion  wasn’t  a  swift victory  for  the British.  However,  this is a

and  instead  relied on  political  outrage  and  diplomatic  pressure.
Numerous  historians,  such  as  Steven  Cook,  assert that  itwas  the  United  States’  stance  against
the  war  that  ultimately  pushed  the  British  out  of Egyptian  domestic  affairs.52  This  is supported  by
documents  from  official  British  cabinet  meetings,  such  as  the meeting  where  they  discussed  their
declining  economic  position,  where  a  highlighted  reality  was  their  need  for  US  economic  assistance
and  their  inability  to obtain  it due  to  their actions  in the  Crisis.53  In  fact, the final  straw  was  when
Eisenhower  didn’t  support  Eden’s  pursuit  of a $1  billion loan  from  the International  Monetary  Fund.54
The  fact  that  the US  played  such  a  big  role in  the  crisis shows  that there  is a dissonance  between
propaganda  and  reality, where  propaganda  consistently  perpetuated  an  inaccurate  image  of Nasser  just
as the  man  who  nationalised  the  Suez  Canal,  but  also  as  the  man  who  successfully  ravaged  the
enemies’  armies  even  under  impossible  conditions.
The  concept  of victory  against  the  powerful  oppressors  after so  many  years  of struggle  was
overwhelming  to Egyptians.  Ahmed  describes  how  “despite  his shortcomings”,  the most  prominent
part  of Nasser’s  “legacy”  in his  memory  is how  he  led  Egypt  against  Britain,  “a  hugely  powerful
country”  and  “overcame”  them.”55  This  again  displays  an underlying  belief  that Nasser  was  the  cause
of  Egyptian  victory  over  the  British  and  French.  Furthermore,  Ahmed’s  words  reveal  how,  in
believing  Nasser  was  the  cause  of  victory,  Egyptians  finally  believed  their capabilities  could  be
expanded,  particularly  after decades  of  failure  to eliminate  repressive  colonialist  presence  in Egypt
with  previous  governments,  because  an  Egyptian  had  led  them  to victory  and  lived up  to  his words.
Mariam  also  comments  that in  winning  the war,  Nasser  had  achieved  “the  impossible”  56 and  how
“overjoyed”57  she  was  at that fact. To  Egyptians,  Nasser  did  not merely  win  the war,  he  revived  Egypt,
belief in Egypt’s  potential  and  pride  in Egyptian  national  identity.
Of  course,  Egyptians  weren’t  completely  ignorant  of the role  of American  opposition.  Mariam
acknowledges  that  the  American  helped  end  the  war.58  Yet,  the specific  diction  highlighted  above
perpetually  reveals  an  underlying  subconscious  belief  in an  exaggerated  view  of  Nasser’s  role.  For
example,  Mariam  discusses  how  through  achieving  victory  under  unfavourable  conditions,  Nasser
restored  “that sense  of hope”  that Egyptians  “could  be  more”.59

The  victory  in the  war  being  deemed  as Nasser’s  victory  was  more  significant  in legitimising
Nasser  than  even  the  nationalisation  of  the  Canal  was.  The  nationalisation  highlighted  Nasser’s
courage  and  lack  of hesitance  to act towards  progress,  unlike  his predecessors.  Yet, as revealed  by the
above  comments,  his  ‘victory’  over  the  aggressors  solidifies  him  as  not  merely  courageous  but
substantively  capable  of  leading  Egypt  beyond  its colonial  past.  This  would  consequently  instil great,
potentially  blind,  trust in Nasser  as a  leader  and  his Arab  Nationalist  ideology  beyond  the Suez  Crisis
to mythological  levels, thereby  intensely.
Thus,  Nasser’s  effort  to  nationalise  the  Canal  was  a  bold  move  that  helped  propagate  his
persona  as  Egyptians  were  overjoyed  simply  to  observe  concrete  action  being  taken.  However,
Egypt’s  victory  in the  war  was  more  significant  as it provided  Nasser’s  words  with  tangible  results
previously  thought  unobtainable  and  promulgated  a new  sense  of  hope  throughout  Egypt  in the
country’s  potential,  cementing  Nasser’s  cult  of  personality  as the  much  stronger  and  more  effective
leader  in  the process.  Yet,  Egypt’s  victory  was  not  a result  of Nasser’s  actions.  Instead,  he  solidified
the idea  that they  were  through  propaganda.  Therefore,  propaganda  painting  Nasser  as the  cause  of
Egypt’s  victory  is what  cemented  his  cult  of personality  and  allowed  him  to become,  as  Anwar  El
Sadat  claimed,  an  “Egyptian  mythological  hero”.60

Costs  of War  and  Battling  the  Colonialists

As  is conventional  for  war-time  propaganda,  Nasser’s  propaganda  glorified  the  costs  of war  as
necessary  losses  to Egypt’s  liberation,  implying  that  propaganda  allowed  Nasser  to palliate  the  costs
of war.  An  example  of this  isin  ‘Sawt  Al  Arab’  (Voice  of  the Arabs),  a nationalistic  radio  program  run
by  the Egyptian  government  which  was  also  widely  popular  over  the  whole  Arab  world.61  Numerous
enthusiastic  speeches  calling  to  Egyptians  “to strike  out  against  the  aggressors”62  aired  frequently,
alongside  Nasser  himself  claiming  it to be  a duty  of the  people  “to  struggle  to get  the  enemy  out  of
their country”63  and  playing  nationalistic  songs.64  Mariam  claims  that in the  aftermath  of the  Crisis,
Egyptians  were  “overwhelmed  with  joy”.65  She  passionately  asserts  the  necessity  of  martyrs  and
glorifies  their deaths  because  “they  died  fighting  for  the freedom  of  their country”.66  Suffering  in war
is intertwined  with  a sense  of the  honour  and  vindication  of obtaining  freedom,  thereby  transforming
that suffering  into  a  source  of pride  in  of itself. Egypt  experienced  the  heaviest  losses  in  the war  on
every  front,  as  it took  place  entirely  on  Egyptian  soil  and  in  Egyptians  towns  that  were  destroyed,67
and  having  the  highest  number  of  casualties.68  Infrastructure  was  badly  damaged  during  the  war,
particularly  when  itcame  to transportation  like  railways,  roads  and  airports,69  a particularly  difficult
setback  for  a  nation  pushing  industrialisation.70  Egypt  opted  to  blockade  the  Canal,  causing  an

However,  this  feature  of  Nasser’s  propaganda  is merely  a  reflection  of  the  context  Egypt
faced.  Nasser  had  committed  a provocative  but  legal  action  in nationalising  the Suez  Canal.72  The  fact
that Eden  had  seen  this action  as a threat  and  was  determined  to destroy  Nasser  and  reassert  British
military  presence  in  the Canal  for it is evidence  that  he  was  an  aggressor  and  a real threat  to Egypt’s
sovereignty.73  Eden  made  many  attempts  to add  a façade  of legality  to his actions  and  present  Egypt  as
the true  aggressor,  with  the British-French  request  for a  ceasefire  between  Egypt  and  Israel  being
intentionally  done  in  a  manner  that  would  weaken  Egypt’s  position  comparatively,  making  it
impossible  for Nasser  to  accept.74  Thus,  it was  Britain’s  own  actions  which  reinforced  the  popular
public  conception  that  it was  stilloperating  under  the apparatus  of an  oppressive  colonialist  state in
Egypt.  Ahmed  observes  how  “Britain  was  being  ridiculous”  in beginning  the  war  “just  because  we
nationalised  something  in  our  own  land”.75  Mariam  also  acknowledges  that “no  one  was  happy  their
country  was  being  invaded,  but  the people  were  ready  to fight”.76 This  notion  was  omnipresent  across
Egypt  and  instigated  a great  deal  of unified  action  amongst  civilians.  Civilians  were  given  guns  and
encouraged  to  fight  themselves,  resulting  in numerous  civilian  makeshift  troops.77  Samir  Ghanem,  a
member  of the  Egyptian  military  intelligence  at the  time,  claimed  “every  Egyptian  was  willing  to
sacrifice  himself  to  defend  his  country”.78  This  may  be  exaggeratory,  given  Ghanem’s  position,
however  these  claims  are  somewhat  supported  by  Mariam,  who  details  how  her brother  attempted  to
get personally  involved  in the  struggle  and  claims  “the  regular  people  were  fighting”,79  “when  faced
with  an  external  threat,  we  unified”.80  Common  cause  was  established  between  Nasser  and  his  people
through  the creation  of a  common  enemy.  The  destruction  of war  was  not  whitewashed,  but rather  the
responsibility  of that  destruction  was  rightly  allocated  to  the real aggressors  rather  than  Nasser,  which
in turn allowed  for that  destruction  to be a symbol  of the resilience  of Egyptian  nationalism.
Nasser’s  power  was  aided  by  the destruction  of  war  as  itallowed  him  to capitalise  on Britain
proving  themselves  to be  the  oppressive  colonialists  Egyptians  saw  them  as. As  with  the  case  of the
nationalisation  of the  Suez  Canal,  Egyptian  state-owned  media  did not  manufacture  the impact  of the
aggressors’  oppression.  Rather,  it constantly  perpetuated  narratives  of it and  capitalised  on  it to
amplify  the  nationwide  sense  of unified  resistance.  Nasser’s  actions  in  creating  civilian  troops  also
had  a  similar  effect.  Hence,  both  Nasser’s  actions  and  propaganda  capitalised  on  anti-colonialist
sentiment,  but  itwas  the actions  of Britain,  France  and  Israel,  both  in the Suez  Crisis  and  previously,
which  created  the foundation  of that sense  in the Egyptian  public  mind.

Conclusion

The  Suez  Crisis  greatly  elevated  Nasser’s  power.  Many  of  Nasser’s  actions  helped  him  maintain  his
power,  such  as the  shocking  defiance  and  strength  he  demonstrated  in nationalising  the Canal  and  his
strategic  decision-making  during  the war.  Often,  Egyptian  unity  with  Nasser  was  effectively  promoted
by  propaganda  surrounding  the  destruction  of  the  war,  but  it was  not  founded  on  itas  anti-Western

the nationalisation  of the  Canal  and  the  myth  of Nasser  as  the man  who  achieved  victory.  The  latter
most  majorly  contributed  to Nasser’s  power  as Egypt  had  failed  for  decades  to do  so,  making  such  a
victory  seem  ‘impossible’.  Thus,  Nasser  ‘achieving  victory’  mythologised  him  and  created  an
overwhelming  sense  of trust  not just  in his courage  but  also in  his infallibility.It also  restored  hope  in
the potential  for Egyptian  greatness  in the  future,  validating  and  popularising  Nasser’s  ideology  of
Arab  Nationalism.  Therefore,  the  presentation  of the  Suez  Crisis  was  more  significant  to Nasser’s
maintenance  of  power  than  Nasser’s  actions.
This  case  study  of Nasser  reveals  much  about  the machinations  of power  for authoritarians  in
post-colonial  states.  Even  after decolonisation,  the  lasting  influence  of Britain  maintained  a sense  of
oppression  in the  Egyptian  public  mind,  and  this  continued  to be  one  of the  most  salient  areas  of
political discontent.  What  was  most  pertinent,  however,  was  not  Nasser’s  real  demonstration  of his
capabilities  through  his  actions,  but  rather  the  perception  of  Nasser’s  ability  to  ‘beat  back’  the
colonisers.  Nasser’s  competency  was  not  a  prerequisite  to  his  popularity  but  was  sufficiently
compensated  by  the  perception  his propaganda  was  able  to promulgate.  On  Nasser,  Fouad  Ajami
comments  that  “the  calculus  of  achievements  and  errors  doesn’t  seem  to  apply  to  charismatic
leaders”.81  Whilst  not untrue,  itis essential  to understand  the context  under  which  this charisma  arose.
It was  not  merely  Nasser’s  charisma,  but  rather  his  strongman  appearance  before  what  Egyptians
believed  to be  an  impossible  enemy,  with  much  desperation  to  find  someone  willing  to fight  back
rather than  rely on  Britain’s  endorsement  to maintain  their  power.

ABSTRACT 

CHARISMATIC LEADERSHIP IN EGYPT: GAMAL ABDEL NASSER 

ALTUN, Tuğba 

M.A., The Department of Middle East Studies 

Supervisor: Prof. Dr. Meliha BENLİ ALTUNIŞIK 

December 2022, 111 pages 

During the years between 1952 and 1970, Egypt was almost the most influential country in the Arab world. Gamal Abdel Nasser’s powerful image in the eyes of the Egyptians and among the Arabs in general as the president of Egypt at that time was influential. Nasser strongly supported Arab nationalism and unity in the Arab world. Also, he was passionately against colonialism and the bipolar system in the world. Therefore, he created a powerful charismatic leadership with his ideas and policies among the Arabs. However, it was interesting to note that he domestic and regional support continued even after the defeats in Yemen and in 1967 War. Thus, this study focuses on understanding how Nasser was able to continue his rule even after the defeats. It is argued that his suppressive policies at home does not explain wholly his popularity in Egypt and beyond. Instead, the thesis claims that the charismatic leadership of Nasser was one of the main reasons for the continuation of Nasser’s rule and his popularity. Therefore, the study suggests that Nasser was able to continue his rule and popularity with charismatic leadership by explaining the features of v

charismatic leadership, Nasser’s domestic and foreign policies, and the process of the establishment of his charismatic leadership. 

Keywords: Nasser, Charismatic Leadership, Egypt, Arab nationalism vi

CHAPTER 1 

INTRODUCTION 

In Egypt, Gamal Abdel Nasser’s priorities focused entirely on Egypt’s political, economic, and social life and the country's independence in every field as the president between 1952 and 1970. In this respect, Nasser made various reforms and worked on closing the gap between the rich and poor, especially with land reform. He advocated Arab nationalism and unity at every opportunity. Also, he supported other countries in their fight against colonial powers. However, Egypt adopted harsh laws that restricted people’s rights and made Nasser the only power which controlled Egypt. He was significantly criticized from that perspective, but he silenced those voices. 

In other respects, Nasser was able to impress many people with propaganda materials such as radio, newspapers, etc. He was an influential speaker who knew what he could talk about to attract people. Therefore, he controlled the media and what people could talk and say about his rule and the coup, ending with “revolutionary” reforms. He advocated “revolution”, the Egyptian role in the Arab world, the Egyptian army and its power, Arab nationalism, and Non-Alignment Movement in the Cold War environment. He was successful in promoting all of those in a sense. 

Nasser began to influence other countries, and many people in those states supported him. There were many victories for Nasser, such as his opposition to the Baghdad Pact, the Czech Arms deal, the nationalization of the Suez Canal, and the establishment of the United Arab Republic (UAR). All these events contributed to Nasser’s reputation in the Arab world, and he became more famous and gained more support. These successes, combined with Nasser's personality, charisma, and propaganda, made him a charismatic leader of his time. He was leading the masses now, contrary to before, and he was an influential leader in every sense. 2

As one of Nasser’s successes, he convinced Lebanon and Jordan not to join Baghdad Pact. Baghdad Pact, established in January 1955, included Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan, Iran, and Britain. Still, Arab League was divided into two groups that went against it, and most of the members supported Nasser. Nasser opposed Baghdad Pact by claiming that it was the work of Western colonialism and challenged the Baghdad pact countries (Heykel 1974, 57–58). Nasser used various tools to challenge the Baghdad Pact, such as radio and newspapers (El-Feth 1965, 270–76). Abdel-Nasser was an influential figure in terms of pushing his agenda to other countries. Thus, his policies prevented Jordan and Lebanon from joining the Baghdad Pact. His charismatic leadership was influential and solid with his ability to impact other countries’ politics and their people. 

Also, Nasser believed Egypt had to maintain independence, so he did not want to be part of any blocs during the Cold War. He participated Bandung Conference in April 1955 and became part of the Non-Alignment Movement. He was an important pioneer figure in this movement. He became a flag and symbol of third-world countries (underdeveloped or developing countries) thanks to his war against imperialism. 

Another success of Nasser was the Czech arms deal. When the US declined Egypt’s request for weapons, Nasser declared that if Western countries continued to decline Egypt’s recommendations, he could agree with other countries. On September 27, 1955, Egypt and the Czech signed an arms deal, which was considered crucial because it proved the independence of Egypt from Western influence (Dawisha 1976, 12–13). This arms deal made Nasser famous among the Arabs because Arabs were not in favor of Western countries because of the colonial past, and if the West challenged someone, they could become the perfect leader choice for them (El-Feth 1965, 279–81). 

Another important event was the nationalization of the Suez Canal. It started with the decision to build Aswan Dam, but Egypt needed budget support. Although the United States, Britain, and the World Bank offered support with some conditions, Nasser hesitated to accept the offer and support because of the conditions (Heykel 1974, 46– 47). After Nasser’s hesitation, the West thought that Nasser could not be suitable for the Western alliance and that he could want to reach a separate agreement with the Soviet Union (Heykel 1974, 68). Then, on September 28, 1956, Nasser declared that 3

Suez Canal Company would be nationalized and Aswan High Dam would be built. After the nationalization decision, France, Britain, and Israel attacked Egypt and restored the international status of the Suez Canal on October 29, 1956. However, the US, the USSR, and the UN broke a ceasefire on November 6, 1956, and all the forces withdrew in March 1957. Nasser won the battle politically and became a national hero (Dawisha 1976, 14–15). 

Later, as a result of a Syrian delegation’s visit to Cairo on January 12, 1958, Nasser was convinced to accept the unity of Syria and Egypt. Nasser decided that a total union should be implemented, and Syria would follow the Egyptian political system. Briefly, Nasser demanded the dissolution of all political parties, withdrawal of the Syrian army from politics; unification of Syrian and Egyptian economies; implementation of state control, and agricultural reform in Syria (Dawisha 1976, 19–20). On February 1, 1958, United Arab Republic was established under the presidency of Gamal Abdel Nasser. Despite Nasser’s reluctance to accept the idea of unity because of the regional and global situation, such as the reaction of Britain, the US, and the Soviet Union and possibly afraid of Arab countries, Nasser made the unity call and be sure that it was shaped by his terms (Dawisha 2003, 186). 

However, many ideologies, groups, or leaders generally have ups and downs. The disintegration of Syria from the UAR was crucial in terms of Nasser’s prestige and the future of Arab nationalism and unity in the region. Therefore, after this incident, Nasser’s charisma and image were harmed. However, he was still an influential leader in the region. He tried to make up for what he lost in the Yemen war, but it became a political and financial disaster for Egypt. Finally, the last challenge was the Arab-Israeli war in 1967 which ended with a big catastrophe for Egypt and the Arab world. 

When UAR was established in 1958, the Baath party was discharged, and its members believed a new state would be built upon them, and the party did not rebel. However, Syria lost its independence and came under the control of Egypt. Also, businesspeople in Syria were not pleased with Nasser’s economic limitations. (Dawisha 2003, 222– 27). After Syria’s decision to withdraw from the UAR, Abdel-Nasser declared that 4

Egypt would not intervene, but it was seen as a hit on Arab nationalism (Dawisha 2003, 231). 

After the UAR’s dissolution, Nasser focused on exporting Egypt’s revolution to the Arab world and consolidating the revolution in Egypt. Also, Abdel Nasser was able to focus more on domestic politics and the political structure of Egypt (Ferris 2012, 28). Also, Nasser became more critical of conservatives who put their interest above national interests after the dissolution of the UAR. For Nasser, Morocco, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, and Lebanon were conservative countries. Because of the dissolution and other countries’ attitudes towards Nasser and unity, Egypt and Nasser got more isolated by that time (Rogan 2017, 275). However, Nasser continued to use the name of the United Arab Republic even after the dissolution. Egypt and Nasser began to support the revolutionary movements of Arabs (Rogan 2017, 385). Egypt used soft power more until 1961, but after the dissolution of the UAR, Egypt under Nasser started to mix soft power with coercion and hard power (Ferris 2012, 57). 

After the dissolution of the UAR and before the Yemen intervention, Egypt was criticized because it intervened in other countries with coups and revolutionary campaigns (Ferris 2012, 8). Yemen was one of Egypt’s retributions to Syria’s withdrawal from the UAR (Ferris 2012, 33–34). For Nasser and Egypt, the Yemen intervention was not calculated right, and it caused unexpected results. Until 1967, Yemen intervention and war-damaged Egypt, and Egyptians started to digress from Arab nationalism. They began to be abstracted from Arab politics and demanded isolation because of the setback in their lives (Dawisha 2003, 234–36). 

Yemen was also a struggle between Egypt and Saudi Arabia between October 1962 and December 1967. For Egypt, this struggle between regional powers was more costly (Ferris 2012, 2–3). Generally, blame or fault of events was put on Saudis and a little Sadat (Ferris 2012, 51–55). Therefore, Saudi Arabia was blamed for the Yemen intervention and seen as an external enemy. In domestic politics, the responsibility for Yemen intervention was in the hands of Anwar Sadat. 5

Finally, on June 5, 1967, the Israeli air force targeted Egyptian, Syrian, Jordanian, and Iraqi airfields. Israel occupied the Sinai Peninsula, Golan Heights, and West Bank. Israeli army forces almost crossed the Suez Canal (Dawisha 1976, 47–50). Egypt was going through an existential crisis besides the conflict with Saudi Arabia and the effects of the Yemeni civil war. Also, there was a struggle in terms of economic and foreign policy problems in Egypt. Therefore, Nasser wanted to solve these problems and consolidate his international relations position. Nasser aimed to develop his image in the eyes of Arab states by going against Israel (Ferris 2012, 268–70). 

After the defeat in 1967, Nasser declared his resignation on June 9. However, Egyptians had significant loyalty to Nasser, and they did not let him resign by taking streets, and Nasser gave up resigning. People believed that Nasser’s resignation would diminish the idea of Arab unity and the possible victory against imperialism and international Zionism(Dawisha 1976, 50–51). On that day, the Egyptian Ministry of National Guidance reported that “Thousands of Egyptians surged through the streets during the warnings about the blackout and air raid. There were 50,000 Egyptians gathered, and they were shouting in favor of Nasser’s leadership.” (Sharnoff 2017, 35). 

Nasser’s prestige was harmed after the defeat of the Six-Day War. Egypt’s economy was not in good condition, and diplomatic relations between Egypt and the United States were at their lowest since 1952. Egypt became more dependent on the Soviet Union. As a result of the defeat, Egypt partially lost regional leadership, its independence from the Cold War, and its truce with Israel (Ferris 2012, 1–2). However, Nasser continued his rule with the support of Egyptians even after 1967. 

As seen by Nasser, charismatic leadership is one of the important aspects of people’s support for a leader, especially during times of crisis. Many different dynamics create and contribute to charismatic leadership, but ideology, purpose, and triumphs are crucial for establishing charismatic leadership. Generally, charismatic leadership is accepted as a positive aspect for leaders, but this matter has a different side. Many people can support charismatic leaders for their policies, reforms, ideologies, and skills. However, these leaders and their administrations have huge propaganda 6

initiatives. Thus, all the things people support can be propaganda for a leader, which the administration establishes. 

Nasser had charismatic leadership, which he built based on people's perceptions. However, as mentioned above, charismatic leadership is not just a positive term for beloved leaders in countries. Leaders or administrations can create charismatic leadership naturally or manually to get people’s support and consolidate power. Therefore, Nasser was a charismatic leader, loved and supported by many Egyptians from different segments of society. Yet, it cannot be said that all Egyptians supported Nasser and his policies and initiatives were always right with his charismatic leadership. 

Also, societies have different segments of people; these people are affected by various events and believe in different things. Therefore, it should not be expected that all the people in a country support the same leader. Also, Gamal Abdel Nasser was not supported by all Egyptians and Arabs during his rule. Nationalists, anti-colonialists, farmers, villagers, and poor people, supported him in a sense, but the middle class, some segments of the military, intellectuals, and traders did not support Nasser entirely (Mansfield 1967, 52–53). 

Nasser oppressed many opposition groups to consolidate his power. Besides, Nasser was an inspirational and influential leader in Egypt and the Arab world, he applied many oppressive domestic policy decisions. Nasser banned all political parties and closed non-governmental organizations. Legislation and the executive were under his control, but there were some regulations for the judiciary not to intervene in politics (Bozbaş 2018, 97–98). Also, Nasser closed parliament and banned political parties, social movements, and religious or secular opposition movements. He attempted to prevent every alternative ideology, person, or group. Even he appointed Al-Azhar sheiks directly (Bozbaş 2018, 43–45). All unions, trade associations, universities, and student and religious groups were under Nasser’s rule (Bozbaş 2018, 197–286). 

As an important propaganda material, the media was under the control of Nasser. He nationalized the press in 1960, and the press focused on limiting independent groups 7

because they did not want anything to harm the regime (Podeh and Winckler 2004b, 19–20). All editors and other vital positions were appointed by Nasser (Bozbaş 2018, 174–75). 

Thus, it can be seen that Nasser was a charismatic leader according to his relationship with his followers and the people's perception. However, Nasser also was considered an oppressive leader. To sum up, it is not necessary to consider charismatic leadership solely a positive term for leaders because charismatic leadership and an oppressive rule can be applied side by side. 

Besides Nasser’s oppressive policies, there were people who supported and liked Nasser on the other hand. Especially some events that contributed to this perception are important. An assassination attempt on Nasser on October 26, 1954, contributed to his powerful stance and charisma and strengthened people’s support for him. When Mahmoud Abdullatif tried to assassinate him, Nasser did not move at all, and the Egyptians saw this behavior as heroic. After this incident, Nasser said that he could sacrifice his blood for his country and its people. Also, he emphasized that his possible death would not matter as long as Egypt could be free (Rogan 2017, 338). Therefore, this was seen as a sign for people to believe in and support Nasser because he was heroic and maybe chosen because he was saved from an assassination attempt. This was accepted as the bond between Nasser and God in the eyes of the people, and even Nasser could reflect this situation like that. 

Regarding the love and support for Nasser, one of the most important proofs was Nasser’s funeral which took place on October 1, 1970. After Nasser’s death on September 28, 1970, and before the funeral, government radios called people to restrain their emotions and behave according to the dignity of their leader’s funeral. Many segments of society – farmers, workers, students, etc. left their villages and towns to participate in the funeral in Cairo. People shouted, “Gamal lives, our blood, and soul for yours, Gamal.” and “You live in our hearts forever, and you left behind your revolutionaries, Gamal.” (du Bois 1971, 45–46). 8

There were people around the region and the world alongside many Egyptians. Millions of people came from different parts of Egypt and the world to say farewell to Nasser at his funeral. Many people were crying and screaming in the footage of Nasser’s funeral (“The Video of Nasser’s Funeral Dirges and Funeral of Gamal Abdel Nasser” 1970). At the funeral, crowds were screaming the name of their passed leader and tried to break through soldiers and policemen to reach his coffin, which was covered with the Egyptian flag. Even the interim president, Anwar Sadat, had a heart attack during the funeral (Anderson 1970). These show how much Nasser was loved by many segments of society in Egypt despite all his coercive policies and defeat in 1967. He was the leader of the Egyptians even when he was buried in the ground in the eyes of his people. 

1.1.Research Objective and Questions 

Gamal Abdel Nasser was an influential leader in the Arab world between 1952 and 1970. He was seen as the leader of all Arabs, not just Egypt, and his influential initiatives, doings, ideology, and speeches impressed many people and countries. Many events contributed to the development of his prestige and charismatic leadership. However, as much as there were events that ended up with positive outcomes, there were events that led to defeats and failures. The most important and influential one was the defeat in 1967 against the Israeli army. 

After that, Nasser lost prestige and charisma in the Arab world despite the continuation of his rule. He and Egypt wished to try to rebuild the Egyptian army and pride with his charisma. Therefore, he continued his rule after such failures and his relatively oppressive regime. Thus, this study focuses on how Nasser could continue to rule even after the 1967 defeat. This study's research question is how Nasser could continue his rule after some failure. On the other hand, the purpose of this study is to understand the effects of Nasser’s charismatic leadership on the continuation of his rule by answering the research question. 

This thesis helps us to see how charismatic leadership can be a solution or tool for a leader in a problematic condition. Generally, studies about charismatic leadership 9

focus on its components, effects, routinization, or specific leaders. In this study, charismatic leadership is accepted and studied as a reason for people’s support and continuation of an administration. In many studies, a leader’s relationship with followers is emphasized. Therefore, this thesis does not indicate all of the reasons why people obeyed Nasser but explains the one possible option, which is charismatic leadership.
