CHAPTER II: LITERATURE REVIEW 

To analyze framings of poverty in cinema, this review of literature commences looking at how poverty was defined in different contexts by different entities, then it sheds light on how poor populations are often framed in cinema, and how that plays out in the Egyptian context. It also examines the role and influence of Egyptian cinema in the 20th century up to 2010. 

2.1. Defining poverty 

This research attempts to analyze the depiction of poorer socio-economic classes in Egyptian film productions over more than half a century. Before examining frames of poverty, identifying what is poverty is an important question for which the answer can be elusive due to the various approaches to defining poverty. 

There are three broad approaches to defining poverty that have been adopted by researchers and policymakers, which center around attempting to measure one of the following: “economic well-being, capability, and social exclusion,” (Wagle, 2002). 

Most commonly used is the economic well-being approach, which is further measured by three different approaches: absolute, relative, and subjective concepts. When looking at poverty, one important distinction that needs to be made is the difference between relative and absolute poverty. When one is described as ‘relatively impoverished’, this generally means they possess much less wealth than other members of society. But this doesn’t necessarily mean that this person is actually poor, as it could be that they’re part of a generally wealthy society, so their Daly, 10 

poverty here is subjective not objective. “A common practice is to define someone as poor if his or her income is less than 60% of the population’s median income,” (Raywat, 2019). 

“Absolute” poverty, on the other hand, is a level of poverty defined in terms of the minimal requirements necessary to afford a basic standard of living. The inability to achieve that minimal standard is considered to be experiencing deprivation and therefore poverty,” (Raywat, 2019). 

When it comes to absolute poverty, a widely embraced definition of poverty that has been adapted by economists and global institutions since 1990 is the poverty line. “Perhaps the most commonly applied poverty threshold, used since 1990, is the so-called global poverty line (GPL), which is delineated by the World Bank. The line is based solely on the cost of living, and is assessed by computing the global prices of key commodities. Up until 2008, the GPL was conveniently defined as one U.S. dollar per day. Anyone making less than this amount was said to be unable to purchase the necessities of life and was thus impoverished. In 2015, due to global changes in commodity prices, that line was redefined as $1.90 per day,” (Raywat, 2019). 

As per the United Nations, poverty is defined as "lack of income and productive resources to ensure sustainable livelihoods; hunger and malnutrition; ill health; limited or lack of access to education and other basic services; increased morbidity and mortality from illness; homelessness and inadequate housing; unsafe environments and social discrimination and exclusion.” 

Extreme poverty, on the other hand, is defined as “a condition characterized by severe deprivation of basic human needs, including food, safe drinking water, sanitation facilities, Daly, 11 

health, shelter, education and information. It depends not only on income but also on access to services,” (Raywat, 2019). 

When poor characters appear on screen, viewers are able to perceive them as poor due to their living conditions and other social and behavioral aspects of their portrayals, not based on theoretical definitions of poverty apply to them. What is significant, however, is why the characters are perceived to be poor, and how their poverty is depicted or framed on screen 

Defining what can be considered as poverty on the screen in an Egyptian context is thus a pursuit integral to this study as it aims to identify how poor people are depicted in Egyptian cinema. A strict, absolute definition of poverty as per global definition is of little help to identifying it on screen, but the discussions of poverty can help guide this study towards what counts as poverty in Egyptian film. Poverty in Egyptian cinema will be looked at through different lenses to be able to identify, as per the scope of this study, poverty depiction on screen. Many aspects will be looked at to conclude if the character under investigation in this content analysis is poor. These aspects were guided by the theory studied, and refined and developed during the pilot study phase of the projects. The aspects considered are namely; their attire, status of job, level of education, place and location of residence, crowdedness of their household and presence of luxury items at their households. This will be further elaborated on in the methodology section. 

2.2.. Framing of underprivileged or minority populations in media 

To understand how this poverty is repeatedly portrayed on the screen and grasp the underpinning social and cultural context of that portrayal, it is useful to look at the framing theory. At its core, the framing theory stipulates that how any topic is presented to the audience (called ‘the frame’) Daly, 12 

influences the choices people make about how to process that information, Media frames of different issues have major impact and implications on how audiences perceive and react to these issues. What makes frames more important to examine, is that they are, “difficult to detect fully and reliably, because many of the framing devices can appear as ‘natural,’ unremarkable choices of words or images,” (Entman, 1991, p. 6). 

These seemingly natural frames end up shaping public opinion, discourse, and even policy towards the subjects of the frames, eventually leading to shaping the living reality of these subjects. A 2011 report by The Opportunity Agenda argues that one of the strongest significant manifestations of frames is how US media has, in news and cinema, consistently framed African American characters in negative frames. Although the tides may be turning, and more positive representations are becoming more widely embraced, the impact of such prolonged and consistent frames is not easy to overcome. “Black males are overrepresented when media touch on certain negative topics, such as criminality, unemployment, and poverty,” (The Opportunity Agenda, 2011). 

These frames end up transcending their medium (television, newspapers, theatre, etc), expanding further to shape the collective public perception about black males, which then negatively impacts their abilities to better their living situations due to the barriers such frame introduce into the collective mindset towards them – even possibly negatively impacting how they perceive themselves. 

“Research and experience show that expectations and biases on the part of potential employers, teachers, health care providers, police officers, and other stakeholders influence the life outcomes of millions of black males, just as their own self-esteem, identity, and sense of Daly, 13 

empowerment affect their ability to achieve under difficult circumstances,” (The Opportunity Agenda, 2011). The way in which the public sees and talks about any population affects policy directed toward the group in question. The might and prowess of framing doesn’t just apply to African Americans, but to most marginalized groups featured in mass media across most countries, including the poor. In a US study by Baumgartner (2008) that traced representation of poverty issues in the media in the second half of the 20 th century found that from the end of World War II and until the 1960s, “the poor were seen as victims of an economic system that had no place for them, trapped in dysfunctional schools, plagued by racial barriers to progress, and a potential threat to social stability and peace if their needs were not addressed,” (Baumgartner, 2008). 

“By the late 1960s, that conversation began to change. So much so that beginning in California and later as a presidential candidate, Ronald Reagan tapped into a widespread feeling that the poor were not deserving of such government generosity […] The poor needed to work harder, to throw off their pessimism about their chances in the American economy, and to free themselves from dysfunctional government programs that encourage laziness, the breakup of families, and dependency. Government policy followed this shift in focus,” (Baumgartner, 2008). 

This paper is then guided by these framing theories to look into how frames of poverty in Egyptian cinema define the lives and opportunities of poor populations. 

Media framing is known to be particularly powerful with illiterate populations. Achieving a high level of literacy, and also a degree of media literacy, enables the audience to be better judges of how media frames work to impact their perception of issues and communities. Daly, 14 

“Individuals who have low educational attainment demonstrated a stronger framing effect than did highly educated individuals,” (Garcia-Retamero & Galesic, 2010). 

Looking at Egypt, where illiteracy rates have consistently been relatively high, the impact of media frames is assumed to be far more powerful than other countries with more literate and media literate populations. As recent as 1996, Egypt’s illiteracy rate stood at 44.4%. In 2017, it had improved to 29.8% (World Data Atlas, 2017). 

It is thus assumed that the power of framing used in relation to poor characters in Egyptian cinema have an oversized impact on how the general public, a big portion of which was illiterate in the 1950s and up to the 1990s. When one doesn’t have the educational ability to distinct fact from fiction, media frames end up being detrimental to how they see the world. This power is assumed to be even more pronounced in the pre-digital media world, when the government was the sole source of information and the sole controller of media, in Egypt and elsewhere. 

To understand the power of frames in Egyptian cinema, a 2010 study detailed how the media frames related to use of hashish/cannabis has impacted public perception and social acceptance of it. Depiction of “hashish/cannabis use’ has witnessed 'a shift in attitude and in the overall depiction of these substances has emerged in more recent films, those produced in the 1990s and after. It suggests that whereas in older cinema these substances were always associated with social and political ills, almost all negative connotations and associations have disappeared in favor of an acceptable and playful depiction.” Perhaps not coincidentally, since the 1990s, “cannabis use (in Egypt) has been the most commonly used by adolescents, and its rates are increasing significantly since 1991,” (Rabie et al., 2020). Daly, 15 

Clearly, there are many other factors that influence the choice of substance use other than media depiction and framing of such use. But, the influence of media framings cannot be ignored. 

This brings us to the questions this study aims to answer; what are the frames applied to poor Egyptians in Egyptian cinema and how did they differ throughout different political and economic eras? 

2.3. Poverty stereotypes in the media 

Misrepresentation of poverty or poor populations in media, whether news or entertainment, is widespread, and has been unchallenged for a long time. Such frames and representations amplify social inequalities and contribute to constructing a misinformed reality of this socio economic segment of society. 

“[Media] stories create a visual sense of reality for the consuming public, and many media critics have begun to call foul for their many misrepresentations of minorities, in particular their over-representation of black poverty. These representations have been shown to have substantial influence on the public’s perception of poverty, which may shape the attitudes and beliefs toward certain policy implementation,” (Smith, 2005). 

A volume of research has been published on the framing of poverty and its implication on constructing social realities and public policies around the world. The lack of such specific research endeavors in Egypt has led the researcher to look elsewhere to build a wider understanding of how poverty is stereotyped in the media across the world. Daly, 16 

Understanding stereotypes used for minorities is important because as Murphy and Ramasubramanian (2014) argue, “Media portrayals often form the primary, if not only, source of social and interactive information about various groups in society. Mainstream mass media have historically marginalized, trivialized, demeaned, and underrepresented minority groups. Consequently, media effects scholars have expressed concern with ways in which audiences use stereotypic media content when forming opinions of people across group affiliations,” (Murphy, Ramasubramanian, 2014). 

In the US, “Quantitative and qualitative studies have examined how the framing of the poor changes public policy or the attitudes of the public or policy elites, often focusing on the discussion of the poor as “deserving” or “undeserving” or on race as a determinant of public support,” (Baumgartner, 2008). 

Bullock, Wyche and Williams, argue that this view of the poor as either deserving or undeserving of public and state assistance and support could be damaging in many ways. In effect, it isolates the poor from the rest of society, presenting their poverty struggle as mostly, if not solely their responsibility and stemming out of their own personal choices, as opposed to public policy and perception toward them. 

Relating these frameworks to Egypt, distinct similarities appear. A main stated goal for the 1952 revolution had been achieving social equality. Monarchy-era’s landowners were seen as corrupt capitalists, and the poor and struggling were seen as the true heroes as far as Gamal Abdel Nasser’s regime and rhetoric was concerned. In that era, sweeping reform gave the poor and middle class in Egypt many rights that were previously exclusive to the rich. They gained the right to free education, healthcare, and employment in the public sector upon graduation. Daly, 17 

These reforms enabled Egyptians to climb up the social ladder in a way that was previously unattainable (Van Bebber, 2021). But, the increasing burden of public expenditure on providing these services, coupled with a booming population and exhaustion of resources in war and propaganda efforts, have led to a decline in the Egyptian economy towards the end of the 1960s, coinciding with the death of Gamal Abdel Nasser in 1970. 

The narrative then changed, and Anwar El Sadat, the following president, adopted another wave of reform that, in essence, reversed some of the elements of the social order established by Nasser. The socialist nature of the state began to slowly disintegrate in favor of a neoliberal system of governance. Exemplifying his policies, Sadat called protestors against lowering bread subsidies ‘thieves’. This was four years before his assassination in 1981. Hosny Mubarak, claiming power shortly thereafter, continued on Sadat’s neoliberal agenda, slowly but surely lessening the state’s role in supporting the poor. In order to do so without losing public support, a shifting of state and media narrative towards poor people ensued, so much so that productions depicting the hardships of poor Egyptians were often accused of ‘damaging Egypt’s image abroad’ during Sadat and Mubarak’s eras (Shafik, 2006). 

“For most people, issues concerning poverty are at a considerable distance from their own daily lives and they primarily gather information about this topic from television, newspapers and the internet,” (Henson et al, 2010). 

Another study by Entman in 1995 “identified two distinct categories used by local and national television to tell stories about poverty: stories that depicted poverty as behaviors that threaten community well-being (e.g., crime, drugs, and gangs) and stories that focused on the suffering of the poor,” (Bullock et al, 2001). Daly, 18 

“Of the 239 analyzed, Entman found that 39% depicted poverty as a source of threat whereas 61% portrayed poverty in terms of suffering.” 

2.4. Poverty and public policy in Egypt 

Poverty exists in different dimensions and can be measured through countless approaches other than merely considering spending income. “While poverty is undoubtedly a problem in Egypt, the measure of its dimension and magnitude is inconclusive,” (Van Bebber, 2021). 

Since the beginning of the Egyptian republic in 1952, poverty-related social policies have taken center stage. Under the socialist regime of Gamal Abdel-Nasser, the once-powerful elite land-owners and colonial actors ceased to be the social strata that the regime targeted to garner support. Instead, Nasser’s social policies, which included free healthcare, education, and guaranteed employment upon graduation, have given way to garnering support from the ‘new middle class’ that Nasser’s policies have created. 

“The raising of minimum wages, social services, investments in agriculture and industry, manufacturing, and the growing power of the army and government contributed to the rise in the rate of social mobility in Egypt during the Nasserist era,” (Van Bebber, 2021). 

It is this social mobility that has transformed the social contract between the government of Egypt and its citizens. The state policies put the poor in the spotlight, and granted them avenues through which they can move up the social ladder, a mobility that had been nearly non-existent under the previous ruler King Farouk. Daly, 19 

Manifestations of Nasser’s policies in arts, music, and cinema are plenty. The poor, including workers, farmers, students, have quickly become the heroes of the era, taking center place in the era’s creative productions. 

For example, the nationalist song ‘ Aash Al Geel Al Sa’ed’ (Long Live the Upcoming Generation), which saw performances by some of the era’s most iconic Egyptian and Arab singers, including AbdelHalim Hafez, Shadia, Nagat Al Saghira, is fully dedicated to empowering blue-collar professions that have traditionally been occupied by poorer populations. In one chorus the song goes ‘Long live the farmer when he feels the sun, spreading its light and growing his crops while he shields and protects it.’ 

It is thus understood that the poor under Nasser were seen as victims of previous elites who hoarded wealth and resources, and seen as an extension of colonial-imposed social structures, depriving poor Egyptians of their basic rights. The poor during the era, which ended in 1971, were glamorized and empowered through state propaganda and generally well-regarded by the regime as they constituted the single most important source of political support to the regime and its policies. 

As a result of massive social expenditure of the era, and the lack of foreign investment, Egypt’s economic growth began to decline towards the end of Nasser’s era, paving the way for a new sociopolitical order under Anwar El Sadat. 

Anwar El Sadat became the president of Egypt in times of turmoil. The economy was in general decline, and the country was in an open state of war with Israel who, in 1967, had invaded Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula along with other territories in Levantine countries. Sadat was Daly, 20 

thus tasked with returning Egypt’s Sinai, which he did through a mix of war and diplomacy efforts, and reorienting the economy and pushing its development. 

One of the first political actions taken under Sadat was the adoption of Egypt’s 1971 Constitution, which remained in effect until the overthrow of Hosny Mubarak in 2011. Sadat came into power promoting and launching what he referred to as the ‘Corrective Revolution,’ bypassing and removing many of the socialist aspects of the previous ruling regime. In 1974, he declared the economic ‘Open Door Policy’ "to free the country's economy from the restrictions that had for so long bound it,” (Baker, 1981). 

For Sadat, Egypt’s economy needed to be liberalized from all the shackles and burdens it had under a socialist approach. He aimed to transform Egypt into a market-economy as opposed to a centrally organized one. Naturally, such efforts meant that the poor were the first to be victimized as a result of such policies. The most striking example of this is the price of bread, an Egyptian household food staple particularly in poorer households. He enacted a policy that aimed at reducing the country’s subsidies of the crucial food item, a policy that was faced with widespread objections. 

“The regime since January 1977 has sought to respond indirectly to the demand to reduce the burden of the price subsidies on the economy. Bread, for example, may stay the same price but it shrinks in size. In 1979-1980 the emphasis was shifted to a "rationalization" of the subsidy policy. Closer examination revealed that reason again meant reduction. But this time was the pool of Egyptians eligible for the subsidies rather than the subsidies themselves that was cut. The divisive social consequences of this kind of economic squeeze were soon apparent,” (Baker, 1981). Daly, 21 

And while cheap bread, free healthcare and education, and guaranteed employment were main features of the Nasserist social era, under Sadat “a ration card was a signal not that certain scarce goods were to be distributed equitably and cheaply but rather that its holder was poor,” (Baker, 1981). “With this measure Egyptians were experiencing the passage from Nasser's socialism to Sadat welfarism,” (Baker, 1981). 

A fast growing population, limited resources and investments, and declining economy, was no longer a sustainable equation. Slowly, everyone was now expected to shoulder the burden of paying their way and making ends meet with waning support from the state. This study aims to assess the degree by which these policies have contributed to a generally unfavorable view of the poor as a burden on the state, a view that persisted through to the next President, Hosny Mubarak, mainly through analyzing the frames applied on poor people in Egyptian cinema. 

President Hosny Mubarak oversaw a period of political and social development that saw many development indicators, particularly those related to Human Development Index (HDI), improve at steady rates in the period between 1981 and 1997, according to a study by Richard H. Adams in 2000. 

Thus, life expectancy at birth, labor and land productivity, and adult literacy, are indicators that saw leaps forward in the era. However, “with respect to poverty, all of the poverty measures used in this study […] suggest that the incidence, depth, and severity of poverty increased in both urban and rural Egypt between 1981-82 and 1997,” (Adams, 2000). 

This is mostly due to the fact that economic growth in Egypt stagnated during the period fell below what is needed to create “labor-intensive economic growth that can raise incomes and reduce poverty,” (Adams, 2000). Daly, 22 

There was also a marked increase in income inequality in the country: “According to the World Bank, the top quintile of earners has increased its share of income since the 1990s, while the bottom quintile has seen its portion of the pie shrink,” (Efrat, 2015). 

And while Mubarak had pursued, at least in name, a policy of economic liberalization and lowering government “control over industry, tourism, financial markets, and oil-production remained in place. The government controls over agriculture were designed to maintain law and order as well as to extract a surplus and thus fund national development. This was also a political technique designed to thwart opposition to the government, as it favored the potentially disruptive urban population by ensuring access to basic food staples at low prices,” (Efrat, 2015). 

In the early 2000s, the government realized that its policies have led to economic strangulation and thwarted growth. So in 2004, “the government liberalized foreign trade and the foreign exchange market as well as domestic price controls. In addition the government embarked on an ambitious program of privatization and financial sector reform,” (Efrat, 2015). 

This worked, as far as macroeconomic indicators are concerned. From 2005 to 2008, the number of new jobs created in the market increased by more than 50% than in 2002/2003. During the same period, “exports of goods and services increased by 75 percent and the stock market doubled, while official unemployment figures fell from 11.2 percent in 2004/2005 to 8.3 percent in 2007/2008. Finally, the country’s external debt was halved and fell to the equivalent of 21 percent of gross domestic product,” (Efrat, 2015). 

These liberalization measures, however, have deeply impacted and effectively lowered the standard of living in Egypt, and contributed to an increased sense of perceived poverty. Daly, 23 

Massive waves of privatizations have also led to economic and social instability, with the country witnessing more than 700 labor strikes in 2007 and 2008 alone. 

When it comes to poverty in Egypt, while the absolute share of poverty (earning less than $2 a day) witnessed a decrease from 17.6% in 1991 to 18.5% in 2005, “for every four poor persons who escaped extreme poverty during 2005- 2008, three initially non-poor persons fell into it,” (Bargawy & Mckinley, 2011). 

2.5. Egyptian cinema: Ownership and financing across eras 

Egyptian cinema is easily the oldest, biggest, most developed and most influential in the Arabic-speaking world. Tracing back to the late 1800s, the country witnessed a number of silent films being produced from as early as 1896. In 1927, the first Egyptian full-length feature, “Layla,” was released, constituting the first stepping stone to establishing a full-fledged media industry. 

Fast-forward to the 1940s and 1950s, Egypt’s cinema industry was flourishing. In the 1950s, according to a report by “The Economist,” Egypt’s cinema industry was the world’s third largest. Beyond its borders, Egyptian cinema had a major cultural impact on Arabic speaking audiences across the whole of the MENA region. 

It was the rise of the middle class in Egypt during the first half of the twentieth century that led to the development of the Egyptian cinema industry as it was then known, according to a 1987 paper by Jane Gaffney. While most early productions of Egyptian films were the effort of foreign communities residing in Egypt, the “‘Egyptianization’ of the cinema was given further impetus in the wake of the 1919 Revolution, which produced a fervor to create national industries and cultural forms,” (Gaffney, 1987). Daly, 24

CHAPTER III: THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK AND METHODOLOGY 

3.1. Framing theory in cinema and public opinion 

This study operates using the main theoretical framework of the framing theory, which, at its core, explains how the media has the power to influence society by the way it chooses to present certain issues and the salience it gives to these issues. In their 1987 study, Gamson and Daly, 29 

Modigliani explain that a media frame is ‘a central organizing idea or story line that provides meaning to an unfolding strip of events.’ 

Public opinion is thus heavily influenced by media frames. Indeed, the public construct views on issues and communities based on how they’re covered in media (Watts et al., 1999). As Scheufele (1999) explained, framing of issues and events in the media can “thus systematically affect how recipients come to understand these events.” 

Framing in the media is done, as Entman (1993), explained that by using certain “keywords, stock phrases, stereotyped images, sources of information and sentences that provide thematically reinforcing clusters of facts or judgments. For scholars, the power of frames can create “a sense of empathy or foster indifference toward a group of people with implications for public policy,” (Evans, 2010). 

Scholars have long suggested, based on evidence from experiments, surveys, and political campaigns that public opinion usually depends on the frames chosen by the elites (Druckman, 2001). 

Therefore, in Egypt’s relatively unfree media environment, frames are not only the sole responsibility or product of the newsmakers or in the case of this study, filmmakers, but also is greatly impacted by the boundaries imposed by the state through its censorship bodies on practitioners in the media and creative industries, particularly filmmaking “due to the wide reach of cinema and its high consumption among Egyptians, there stemmed a need for regulation to establish control over what can be viewed or expressed through film,” (El Adl, 2014). 

It would, however, be unfair to claim that censorship of art began in Egypt with the establishment of the army-led republic in 1952. As El Adl explains, it was under the rule of Khedive Ismail (1863-1879) when the establishment of Cairo Opera House led to an exponential Daly, 30 

increase in theater bands and performances, which in turn have started heavily influencing public opinion when it comes to political issues. “The state then realized the importance of controlling content,” (El Adl, 2014). 

The implications of such state control over creative content, which has been greatly tightened under Gamal Abdel Nasser, who, in 1963, nationalized the whole cinema industry, means that the framing of issues and events in Egyptian cinema was inadvertently heavily impacted by the state’s own policies and agendas. When it comes to the poor, a cornerstone of Nasser’s reformist and socialist agenda, framing theory can help understand how films of the era, and the eras that followed in which the state continued the same censorship practices with varying degrees, positioned poor people in relation to others in society and to the state. Framing of a particular community doesn’t only impact policies and opinion towards them, but has the power to influence and indeed define how these communities view themselves. 

It is thus assumed that the frames used to depict poor people and other social segments in Egyptian cinema are not mere coincidences. Depictions that appear in films in Egypt often go through vigorous censorship, in a continuous effort to keep the content of films in line with the agenda of the regime, and hence this effort is seen by the researchers as an attempt on part of the state via filmmakers to set the agenda for the public discourse on poverty and poor people. In other words, this is known as cultural agenda setting, which is the “transfer of salience from the media to the public also applies to the case of cultural products or, more broadly, cultural objects such as works of art, artists, and cultural organizations,” (Symeous et al., 2015). This is further elaborated in the coming section. 

3.2. Agenda setting theory Daly, 31 

The agenda setting theory was first introduced in 1927 by Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw. Its main premise is centered around understanding how the media sets the agenda for the public by focusing on certain issues, and in its second level, informs the audience on how to think about these issues. In other words, the media tells the audience what to think about and how to think about it. 

In their choice on how to display information, media practitioners, from journalists to filmmakers, ‘play an important role in shaping political reality,’ (McCombs, 2003). 

The media thus plays an important role in shaping public discourse, discussion and policy towards issues and communities, including issues of poverty. In this research, we aim to understand how Egyptian films, which has seen varying but mostly acute levels of censorship during the period under investigation (1955-2010), have portrayed citizens of low socio-economic class, and how this depiction has helped 

“Agenda setting occurs through a cognitive process known as ‘accessibility,’ which implies that the more frequently and prominently the news media covers an issue, the more that issue becomes accessible in the audience’s memory,” (Iyengar & Kinder, 1987 in Freeland, 2012). 

Agenda setting can happen on many different levels, one of which is what is referred to as Policy Agenda, which “deals with how media and public agendas might influence the decisions of elite policy makers,” (Freeland, 2012). 

With film having historically been a major influencer in Egyptian media landscape, with consecutive governments enacting censorship practices that ensure that film content is in line Daly, 32

It is then assumed that the agenda for filmmakers is set by the state in an indirect way, and filmmakers go on from there to create productions that set the agenda for the public and policy makers in a way that is consistent with the messages the state aims to disseminate. In a way it is a closed feedback loop that defines the living realities of Egyptians in very concrete ways.

3.5. Frames 

This study analyzes how movie makers across different eras framed poor characters, studying this depiction through three broad frames that are further broken down into smaller, more objectively observed, categories. These frames are namely whether the poor character was depicted to be honest or dishonest, a hero or a villain, and how accountable he/she is for his/her poverty. 

As Talib explains (2015), clothing or attire (or lack thereof) constitutes a major component in how a person is perceived, and whether they are perceived to be poor or otherwise. In Egypt, urban centers often have the highest concentration of high-income individuals, and poverty is more densely concentrated in poorer areas, (Roushdy, Assaad, 2007). This is why Daly, 35 

when attempting to identify if the character is poor, we look at their attire and whether it is clean, well put-together, or has clear ribs or dirt on it, hence indicating a degree of poverty. 

Another factor that was developed to identify poverty is whether the character lives in a rural or urban setting, with the rural population assumed to lean more towards being poor. If in an urban setting, the formality and informality of the setting is analyzed, as slums today constitute a major component of urban life in Egypt, with residents of slums typically being of lower socioeconomic status. It is thus assumed that if a character has a rural dialect, it would count towards them being perceived as poorer as if they have an urban (Cairene) accent. 

Education and job status are another factors we analyzed to reach a conclusion about the socioeconomic status of the character. The higher the level of education, the less likely they are to be poor. The lower the status of job, the more likely they are to be poor. 

Lastly, and importantly, if the character directly refers to themselves as struggling with money or being poor, or is directly referred to by others as such, then the character is counted as poor. 

Once a character is identified as poor, an analysis of frames is conducted, measuring hero/villain, honest/dishonest, and accountability of poverty frames. This is why the hero/villain and honest/dishonest frames were introduced into this analysis, in order to be able to shed light on the presence of such dichotomy when it comes to the depiction of poor and rich characters. It is assumed that under the socialist era of Nasser, poor people were more likely to be depicted as honest heroes, and in neoliberal eras of Sadat and Mubarak, this representation is assumed to have been reversed. 

When it comes to the accountability of poverty, it is crucial as explained by Baumgartner (2008), how issues of poverty are portrayed in the media, and one of the most important elements in these portrayals is what the poverty is portrayed to be caused by: personal shortcomings or dysfunctional socioeconomic policies. When it’s the latter, audiences are compelled into sympathizing with the poor characters, but when they’re seen as failures whose poverty is a result of their own shortcomings, public perception change, which can lead to a change in policies and rhetoric towards poorer segments of society.

3.5.a. Accountability of poverty 

One major view people have towards poverty, and that ends up determining their attitude towards poor people, whether depicted on screen or in real life, is the reasons why they’re poor. It could be a myriad of reasons, but at its core, are the poor blamed for their poverty or seen as victims of sociopolitical ailments and inequalities. To investigate this frame, the researchers are dividing it up into two main components: deserving and undeserving, and deficit/grit/structural ideologies, these are further elaborated on below: 

Deserving/Undeserving poor frame: 

Attitude and beliefs towards poor people vary across countries, but common threads in public perception are evident. Generally, the poor are seen in public perception as ‘deserving poor’ and ‘undeserving poor.’ In the US, this dual stereotype rose in prominence in the 1960s and 1970s, and while in the 1950s, the deserving poor narrative dominated, the ‘undeserving poor’ narrative took hold henceforth, leading to existential changes in America’s welfare system and social policies toward the poor. The ‘undeserving poor’ narrative has seen resurgence since the 2008 financial crisis (Tihelkova, 2015). ‘Deserving poor’ perspective includes children, the sick, and the old, i.e. individuals unable to do work, therefore deserving of state intervention and support. Undeserving poor, on the other hand, refers to able-bodied unemployed of all kinds (Tihelkova, 2015). This analysis will investigate the presence of the deserving/undeserving dichotomy through the lens of physical ability. If the poor is depicted as young, senior, or ill, they will be counted as deserving, undeserving if adult and healthy. 

Depictions of poverty do not merely stem from the agenda of the filmmaker or the producer, but are often due to a deeply-ingrained ideological view of poverty in real life. There Daly, 38 

are those who generally view the poor as lacking in ambition, skills or desire to better their lives, and are poor mostly due to his/her shortcomings.. In this case, the person with this view adheres to what is referred to in this paper as deficit ideology (Gorski 2008a; Sleeter 2004; Gorski, 2016), or deficit frame. It is the most dominant ideological perspective of poverty (Gorski 2016). A closely related but widely different ideological perspective is grit ideology, when the poor person is viewed as someone with ‘personal attributes that enable [him/her] to overcome adversity that might overwhelm others.’ In other words, the poor here are viewed as hustlers and can-do people. 

The issue with these two ideological perspectives is that they essentially blame the poor’s condition on the poor, not accounting for structural vulnerabilities such as lack of education, lack of access to the job market, or economic and social policies that disadvantage the poor and can cause poverty to be endemic in certain populations or areas. It is thus assumed that if such an ideological perspective or frame is depicted within these two ideologies; deficit and grit, it would essentially mean an unfavorable frame in case of deficit, and mildly unfavorable in case of grit. This distinction is due to the fact that even though both frames view the poor as complicit or causing their conditions, the grit ideology is the view of the poor with some positive qualities like independence and resilience. 

The third and final ideological perspective related to the role a poor person plays in their economic status is structural ideology or frame (Galdwin,1967). In this perspective, the poor are viewed as a victim of structural deficit in society or economy that puts them at a disadvantage, and are thus viewed as victims of social and economic inequality. This perspective will be considered a favorable one as it accounts for the role of state, society, and public policies in creating or helping dismantle impoverishment. Daly, 39 

The three ideological perspectives (frames) are further elaborated on below: 

● Deficit frame: Deficit frame is used to depict the character as inable to think about or plan for the future. He writes that poor individuals are “unable or unwilling to plan for the future, to sacrifice immediate gratification in favor of true ones, or to accept the disciplines that are required in order to get and to spend [money]” (Banfield, 1970). “Certainly, there is no shortage of evidence that deficit ideology has commonly been perpetuated throughout history to maintain power for the wealthy, and ensure the poor stay poor.” 

● Grit frame: According to Gladwin (1967) “If poverty is both the cause and result of a way of life in which self-defeating behaviors are learned by each rising generation, then any attack on poverty should try to modify these behaviors [...] if the cycle is to be broken, poor people must among other things be taught new and more effective ways of functioning,” (Gladwin, 1967, p. 112). 

● Structural frames: These frames portray poverty as an outcome of disadvantages as attributable to “economic injustice, exploitation, and inequity,” (Galdwin, 1967) and not the character’s responsibility or fault. 

Combining these three ideological perspectives with the dichotomy of deserving/undeserving poor is assumed to present a clear image on how poor main characters are depicted in Egyptian films and how sympathetic the creators are towards their economic situation. Sympathy is not significant in and by itself, but it does indicate whether state policies should interfere to support poorer people. Portraying the poor as victims of their economic situation translates into the need for favorable economic policies and financial support of the state, in the form of subsidies, pensions, healthcare and other forms of financial aid; a direction popularized under the Nasser Daly, 40 

regime. On the other hand, portraying them as able adults who are too lazy to grind and escape poverty, translates into freeing the state from responsibility towards them, a direction that became more popular under subsequent regimes. 

3.5.b. Hero/Villain 

In the film’s main conflict or storyline, the hero is the one who represents the good side of the fight. In Egyptian films, such as classic Hollywood films, the hero ends up defeating/catching the villain, (Indick, 2007). Typically, viewers sympathize with and identify with heroes due to their perceived positive moral qualities, (Tobon, 2018), such as honesty and purity of intention even if sometimes actions are flawed. 

The villain on the other hand, is generally the ultimate source of evil or struggle in the film. They are seen as villains not just for being guilty for committing wrongdoings, but for the presence of the following traits in addition to being guilty: ‘intentionality, consequential (harmful) action, and causal responsibility,’ (Bartels et al., 2015). 

This dichotomy is chosen because before the 1952 Free Officers movement, most Egyptian films were of an escapist nature. And while the movement “didn’t immediately transform the structure of the Egyptian cinema industry [..] it create a climate in which new themes of a sociopolitical nature could be dealt with on screen,” (Gaffney, 1987). Chief amongst these themes were plots and films pertaining to heroes, typically of nationalist inclinations. Themes emerging in that era idolized heroes who fight occupation, corruption and capitalism, in line with the new regime’s socialist agendas. As a socialist regime, Nasser’s policies and speeches spoke to previously unaddressed segments of the population, like workers, peasants, rural Egyptians, among others. Films of the era followed suit, idolizing poorer Egyptians whose Daly, 41 

struggle had been seen as a result of the rich and the colonizers under the monarchy, and thus the presence of the hero-villain dichotomy was evident. 

Accordingly, five aspects will be investigated to decide on the presence or absence of the hero/villain dichotomy. The first will be whether they intentionally inflict harm upon others or, conversely, prevent harm from others. Second will be their tendency to stand up to injustices regardless of consequences, third is their tendency to help others in need or, conversely, ignore them. Being hot or cool tempered will be looked at next, and finally how giving and generous they are with their possessions. 

3.5.c..Honesty/Dishonesty 

Similar to the hero/villain dichotomy, the propaganda machine produced by the 1952 revolution was consistent in depicting the poor and struggling in a positive light. They were seen as honest, modest, and would not commit wrongdoing even if it would help end their financial struggles. It was often the honesty of the protagonists that was rewarded at the end of the films with a happy ending in which they get to live happily ever after, or come into great wealth. In the films of the era, and even in the monarchical era that preceded it, the ending always came with the good, honest, triumphing over the evil and dishonest. It was an unspoken contract between the viewer and the filmmaker that a happy ending is guaranteed, and that the wrongdoings, top of which is conniving, plotting, and dishonesty, will be punished. Films of a realist nature that emerged in the late 1970s and 1980s didn’t necessarily stick to this formula. With the open door policy and the liberalization of the economy, it was those who managed to make the most money that were idolized and granted respect. This draws parallels to Anwar El Sadat describing citizens protesting his hiking of bread prices in 1977 as ‘thieves,’ signifying the end of the social contract Daly, 42 

that implies that state is responsible for feeding the poor, and the start of a new one which sees demanding such support from the state as an attempt at theft. This is why the honest/dishonest dichotomy is investigated through this framing analysis. Honesty will be investigated through different categories, including lying, stealing, taking bribery, and conning others. This analysis attempts to show whether honesty frames have, as hypothesized, been attached more prominently to poor characters under the socialists regime of Nasser, and whether that has changed under the economically liberal regimes that followed.

# CHAPTER IV: DATA ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS 

This analysis set out to measure four main things; representation of poverty amongst main characters; accountability of poverty (i.e. reasons attributable to poverty within the context of the film), hero/villain frame, and honest/dishonest frame. In many cases, the results fall in line with the assumptions outlined by the researchers on how each of the president’s ‘poverty policies’ impacted filmmaking in their eras, but in others, they contradict these assumptions and therefore stand to be further scrutinized to understand how these findings emerged. Daly, 61 

RQ1: What is the representation of poor characters among main characters in Egyptian films between 1955 and 2010 and how does it compare across different political eras? 

To analyze the representation of poverty in main characters across different eras of Egyptian cinema, the researchers looked at different aspects that define poverty in an Egyptian context. First and foremost, characters that directly referred to themselves, or were referred to by others, as poor, were counted in this analysis as poor. This is based on the assumption that the audience will come to view the character as it identifies itself regardless of the character’s living conditions. When these two conditions weren’t met, the researchers then looked at their level of education, status of job, attire, place and location of residence, overcrowding of households, presence of leisure and luxury items at households. After applying this methodology to main characters in all 18 films studied, it was found that the overall representation of poverty in Egyptian cinema in the period from 1955 to 2010 was at about 22 out of 41 main characters. This indicates that poor characters were generally over-represented in cinema, with the latest poverty rate Daly, 62 

released by CAPMAS in 2020 being 29.7% - while the percentage corresponding in the study is 55.5%. This indicates that poverty or poor Egyptians is a topic of interest to filmmakers and production companies in Egypt, leading to this overrepresentation of poor characters. This could be due to many reasons; attempting to influence policy; attempting to empower poor populations; or could simply indicate that filmmakers wanted to appeal to masses of society to generate revenue by depicting stories that resembled their lives and aspirations, particularly due to the fact that commercialism has long been a dominant feature in Egyptian cinema production. 

In the six films produced during Gamal Abdel Nasser’s era (1955-1969), a majority of main characters, seven out of 12 main characters, were depicted to be poor, reflecting the regime’s own rhetoric towards poor Egyptians, who were seen as the main supporters of the socialist regime as opposed to the rich elite that was targeted in sweeping nationalization and anti-capitalist reform. Nasser was widely proclaimed to be ‘president of the struggling – Za’eem E Ghalaba’ , and much of the support for his policies came from those at the lower end of the socio-economic spectrum. This is a potential explanation to why main characters were overwhelmingly poor during his era, an era in which the state exercised tight control over film and media content, and even used the country’s media prowess to further its policies in Egypt and across the world. The question here remains whether those portrayals were more positive in nature than negative, showcasing poor people as honorable, honest, heroic, and deserving of support. This will be discussed under the second research question this study looks at. 

The poor in Nasser’s era films were mostly belonging to the ‘urban lower class’, with only one case of a rural lower class main character appearing in the 1968 film Ana El Doctor (I’m the Doctor). Interestingly Ibrahim, the poor character in this production played by Farid Shawky was pretending to be a doctor, a typically urban profession that implies a high degree of education, to fool the residents of his village into seeking him for medical advice and paying him for it, even going to the length of lying to them and making them feel that they are sick while they’re not so they continue to pay for his services, effectively taking advantage of the perceived naivety of his village natives – a stereotype often associated Daly, 63 

with rural Egyptians. He eventually, as is the case with most Egyptian films of the era where the good often triumphs over evil, is finally revealed for who he truly is and is sentenced to prison time. 

Anwar El Sadat, was leading Egypt during a critical transitional period in which he presided over policies that aim to alter the socialist nature of governance in Egypt and adopt a liberal economic approach in which the state sought-after to lessen the public support on it in offering subsidies on goods and services. One of the most significant events of Sadat’s rule was the 1977 uprising, which followed an attempt of hiking the price of bread in the market – a staple in Egyptian cuisine and long seen as the ultimate subsidy for the poor. Sadat’s security apparatus crushed the protest, and he then called the uprising ‘The Revolution of the Thieves,’ starkly highlighting his differing approach to poorer Egyptians than Nasser. This was very evident in the six films studied in his era, where main characters were only recorded as poor in five out of 12 main characters of our sample. While this remains higher than official poverty rates during his era, it was the lowest representation of poor characters amongst all three eras studied. 

In film productions under Sadat, the poor were often depicted to be of the urban lower class, and mostly occupying informal professions. In the 1979 production Al Motwahsha (The Savage) starring Egyptian cinema icon Soad Hosny in the role of the poor showgirl Baheya who falls in love with the bourgeoisie man Ashraf. They attempt to be together and get married, but she’s instantly rejected by his social circles and family, ending up leaving him and her job and taking up a factory job to better her situation. She eventually makes it back to show business, and as he attempts to get her back and the film comes close to ending on a happy note, she is killed by a band member who disapproves of their relationship because he had grown attached to Baheya. The film exemplifies the class struggle in Egypt under Sadat, with the poor unable to escape their poverty and even seen as undeserving of happiness by fellow lower class citizens, a stark difference from the honorable cooperation and well-wishing amongst the poor in earlier productions. Daly, 64 

Starting 1981, Hosny Mubarak became the president of Egypt, a position he will maintain for nearly 30 years. Mubarak, previously Sadat’s Vice President, followed in the latter’s footsteps in adopting neoliberal policies that aimed at reducing state support to poorer populations and to gradually lift subsidies – a pursuit that was never fully actualized. Mubarak’s era saw unprecedented freedoms in filmmaking, with films seen as directly critical of state policies emerging during the era, depicting deteriorating socio-economic conditions in the country. This can be a reason why poverty representation in main characters increased from the era of Sadat, reaching 10 out of 15 main characters of the six films included in the sample. Towards the last quarter of his rule, Mubarak allowed unprecedented creative and political freedoms in order to appease his Western critics and appear democratic – this led to an influx of movies criticizing corruption, social inequality, and police brutality. These themes emerging strongly in Egyptian cinema possibly contributed to higher representation of poor characters during his era. 

An example of how poverty was depicted towards the end of Muabrak’s rule is the film ‘Welad Al Balad’ which was released in 2010. It revolves around a group of youth working in informal jobs and seeking to migrate to seek better job opportunities and escape poverty. They get entangled with a corrupt politician who is portrayed to be a spy to a foreign entity - which is the turning point at which they decide to drop all their migration plans and pursue the spy until he’s caught. They eventually redisvoer their love for Egypt and the film ends on an nationalistic tone with Egypt winning a football match and all the cast finding themselves cheering in the street, rediscovering their love for their country beyond all their basic needs, and despite the fact that their conditions remain unchanged. The film emphasizes the message that the state isn’t particularly responsible for making anyone’s life better, and that despite any hardships or inequalities, loving Egypt should remain above all without any doubt or question. This depiction was common during the last quarter of Mubarak’s rule, and at its essence it deprioritized real-life issues of poverty and created an image in which the country should be loved no matter what and without any expectation of the state caring for the poor. Daly, 65 

RQ2: How did Egyptian media films frame poor characters between 1955 and 2010 and how do they compare between eras (1952-2010)? 

The frames analyzed in this study focused on the depiction of poor people across three main frames; honesty versus dishonesty, hero versus villain, and accountable versus unaccountable for their poverty. 

Accountability of poverty: Daly, 66 

One crucial frame under investigation in this study is the accountability of poverty frame. It is of great importance to the scope of this study to examine how films depict the reasons for the poverty of poor characters. The perception of characters as responsible for their poverty or victims of unjust circumstances is a crucial frame that ends up defining and shaping public policy towards poor people in real life, and whether they deserve state support. If the poor are seen as victims of structural injustices, and unable to fend for themselves in an unequal system, that influences policy and pushes it in the direction of increasing the state’s role in supporting poor people through subsidies. If they are otherwise seen as lazy, corrupt, or greedy, they are then perceived to be undeserving of support and basically victims of their own making. 

This frame is a combination of two constructs, deserving and undeserving, which is mostly concerned with looking at the physical abilities and health of the characters, and whether they are Daly, 67 

physically able to put in the labor to escape their poverty. The other component is whether their poverty is seen through the deficit, grit, or structural frames which are elaborated on in the methodology section. 

Overall, and alarmingly, poor characters were depicted accountable for their own poverty, with 17 out of 22 of total poor characters being depicted as undeserving and under either the deficit or grit framework – meaning they are either incompetent or unwilling to better their situation (deficit) at 11 characters, or working hard to try to escape their situation (grit) at six characters. While these two frames seem contradictory at first, they actually are closely interlinked in that they both blame the poor for their own poverty, and shift the focus instead on what the poor person is doing to escape their poverty. The structural framework, appearing in four characters, on the other hand, places the poor as victims of social and economic injustices and inequalities, thus attributing their poverty to policies and conditions that are outside of their own control – which is more often than not reflective of the socioeconomic reality where rich people get access to education and work opportunities that enable them to continue being rich, and poor people are denied access to resources that enable them to escape their poverty, regardless of their attitude towards their own situation. 

As expected, films during the Nasser era mostly viewed the poor as undeserving and attributed their poverty to structural inequalities in three out of the seven characters analyzed in that era. This goes to show that Nasser’s socio-economic policies translated to an on-screen glorification of poor people, and viewed them as victims of the corrupt, rich elite. One iconic film from Nasser's era that happened to be included in the sample of this study is Nahnu La Nazra’ Al Shawk (We Don’t Plant Thorns) by the well-known actress and singer Shadia. Her character is depicted to be illiterate, having gone through a rough childhood where she was continuously abused by her stepmother during her father's life and after his death, and then forced into unpaid labor in service of her grandmother and her new family. As she attempts to build a new life and is lucky to have attained employment as a housekeeper at a relatively well-off family household, where she falls in a mutual love relationship with their eldest son, she is then faced by structural societal barriers to actualizing her dreams of marrying him, with him having to wed Daly, 68 

another woman more of his status and closer to his family's social class. She is then thrown into a life of misery where she weds and loses her only child, before she eventually dies while trying to save the son her only love had with his wife. The movie is striking for its representation of structural causes of poverty, showcasing how the lack of education and access to the job market could constitute impenetrable barriers for the poor to better their living situations. Audience would finish the film with a great deal of sympathy towards her, acknowledging how much of her misfortune was indeed outside of her control and how she had been truly been a victim of society and, implicitly, the state. A raw and sincere depiction of this magnitude isn't seen again throughout this study, during Nasser's era or otherwise. 

Though the structural frame was the single most common category, the two other categories of deficit and grit were also featured prominently, though each less on its own, both combined to be over half of characters depicted, at two out of seven characters each, for a total of four characters. This could be an indication to how these frameworks aren’t entirely just products of policies or filmmakers’ agendas, but they are generally-held views by large swaths of society towards poverty. Frames, as is known, are often not entirely manufactured based on an agenda (which can also happen), but are often exaggerated aspects of reality - as in these frames of poverty in deficit and grit frameworks have indeed emerged from these views being present in society, which are then overly emphasized in creative productions and news reporting. Furthermore, the general public often see issues of poverty in isolation of themselves and their everyday lives, despite Nasser’s socialist policies that have translated in more films attributing poverty structural causes than any other era, the deficit and grit frames still featured prominently simply due to the fact that they are strongly present in the collective mindset in the wider society. 

Transitioning to the neoliberal phase under Sadat, poor characters were mostly depicted to be responsible for their own poverty, with four out of six characters falling under undeserving/grit and undeserving deficit combined. Characters that were poor due to structural reasons were recorded 40% of the time. Daly, 69 

During Mubarak, the deficit framework reigned supreme, with six out 10 characters seen as deficit, and so portrayed to be incompetent and unwilling to change their situation. One character was seen as physically unable to work towards a better situation, while four characters were seen healthy enough to work towards bettering their situation but simply lacking the desire or willingness to – therefore undeserving of support from the state or otherwise. In the six films studied, two characters were seen as unaccountable for their poverty, and poor due to structural reasons. Again, the dominance of these two frames (deficit, grit) during Sadat and Mubarak’s eras despite the openness and lessened censorship that marked the beginning and end of Muabrak’s era, could be attributed to the fact that these frameworks (i.e. perspectives) exist in society and the media at large. Most Egyptians living under Mubarak were born in slightly before or during the beginning of the neo-liberal phase which Sadat initiated and Mubarak continued, meaning that throughout their lives, they were exposed to perspectives and opinions in public and in the media that place poverty within these frameworks as a result of neoliberalism which emphasizes individuality over the collective - as in every person is responsible for their own fate and their actions determine their destiny - as opposed to the structural framework which acknowledges that despite one’s best intentions and efforts, structural barriers could still make them unable to lift themselves out of poverty (i.e. lack of high quality education, healthcare, access to high-paying jobs, etc..). 

Hero/Villain Frame: Daly, 70 

Generally, across all films under investigation in this study, the presence of the hero/villain frame was somewhat balanced, with slightly above third (eight characters) being portrayed as heroes same percentage for normal depictions, meaning neither hero nor villain, and villain frames appearing in six characters in all films analyzed.

Despite his poor condition, he rejects all her attempts and stays true to his one and only love, opting instead to work harder and pool some money to buy his own lorry to make his situation better. Conversely, the “Devils of the Daly, 71 

Night” film by the same actor, Farid Shawky, released during Nasser’s era, depicts Shawky as a poor character during the time of the 1919 revolution, i.e. before the era of Nasser and during the monarchy. Interestingly, the character is here depicted as a villain, with his main occupation being a thug who collects fees from prostitutes in order to protect them. The stark contrast between depictions of a hero poor person living under Nasser, and a villain poor person living under the monarchy, speaks volumes on how the general atmosphere towards poverty and poor people was at the time of Nasser’s enforcing his socialist agenda which filtered down to every aspect of society, from employment to education to filmmaking, while simultaneously depicting poorer population living under the monarchy as left with no choice but to embark on immoral pursuits to achieve a dignified life. 

Surprisingly, during Anwar El Sadat’s era, the hero frame appeared three out of five characters time – more than Nasser’s. But this could be attributed to the fact that representation of poor characters was generally lower during that era, combined with the relatively small sample size. The first film analyzed during Sadat’s era, “The Clock Ticks at Ten,” offers a wildly different portrayal of the poor character. The main protagonist is indeed depicted to be poor; however he is also a college student who is working as a chauffeur for a rich family so that he can make ends meet. He is depicted as neither villain nor hero, but rather through a normal frame where he sometimes does things right and also makes some grave mistakes. However a main feature of his situation is that he is striving to make his situation better by taking up informal employment while continuing to study to achieve a level of education sufficient for a more comfortable life. This brings to light how values such as self-reliance and independence were emphasized and prioritized. Furthermore, the fact that Sadat’s era witnessed more hero frames than the socialist era, coupled with the finding that characters had mostly been framed under the deficit/grit frameworks, it can be inferred that while the narratives depicted poor characters as deserving of their poverty, they attributed heroic features to them in order to, again, emphasize the individuality of each person in their struggles of poverty, and that despite their struggles, they still aim to do good by those around them - this glorification of poverty that implies the state isn’t responsible for it is seen by the Daly, 72 

researchers as dangerous and misleading as it does in effect shape a perspective that one should sacrifice and struggle without demanding more. 

A more balanced picture appears when looking at the hero/villain frame during Mubarak’s era, where three characters weren’t depicted in either hero nor villain frame, and hero and villain frames both appearing in two out of four characters each. This could be attributed to the rise of Realist film themes in the 1980s and, and films of new sociopolitical themes towards the last quarter of Mubarak’s rule that captured socioeconomic realities in a manner that was impermissible by censorship bodies before. Generally, not much could else be deduced from the hero/villain frame during Mubarak and Sadat’s era. 

Honest/Dishonest Frame 

Honesty is one important component the researchers sought to investigate in relation to poor main characters in Egyptian films. Across all eras, an equal representation of honest versus dishonest frames was found, at 19 characters each. Four characters were found to be neither honest nor dishonest. Daly, 73 

When it comes to the era of Gamal Abdel Nasser, most characters were found to be acting dishonestly in one or more scenes of the film, at seven out of 12 characters . In the films studied under Sadat, most characters were found to be acting in an honest manner at 12 out of 14 characters. Mubarak’s era saw 10 out of 15 characters acting dishonestly. 

These results go against the assumption of the researcher that poor characters under Nasser were depicted in a positive (i.e. honest) light. The researchers attribute this to the small size of sample used in this study, and further analysis using bigger samples might be more revealing when it comes to studying the honesty and dishonesty frames applied on poor characters in Egyptian films. 

State-owned Vs privately-owned productions 

Aiming to achieve a degree of balance between private and state owned production, the researchers picked a random sample of state-owned productions from the Nasser and Sadat era. After investigation, no significant diversion emerged between both kinds of productions. Seeing that Nasser had initiative far-reaching censorship apparatus over film content, that was, to varying degrees, maintained in following eras, it could be argued that such state control over film content resulted in producing films that are in line with the state’s policies and agendas, rendering the difference between these types of productions insignificant. Another reason, which is a general limitation of this study, could be the small sample size (eight private versus four state productions during Nasser and Sadat). Further investigation is needed using bigger samples to understand if significant differences could potentially be present. Daly, 74 

CHAPTER V: CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION 

This study set out to investigate the representation and depiction of poor characters in Egypt cinema over a decade, a field of study that has rarely been explored before. Through this analysis, it was found that poor characters are overrepresented in Egyptian cinema between 1955 and 2010, and the researcher attribute that to many factors that include the state’s own policies towards promoting stories and narratives of poor people who were seen at the socialist era as the most significant constituents, and possibly the desire of filmmakers to appeal to mass audiences given the commercialism that has dominated the Egyptian cinema since its inception, and therefore its reliance and focus on generating profit. In latter eras, the researchers attribute this over representation to the relatively free media environment that have created an environment conductive to discussing social issues and ills, and spotlighting the struggles of the underprivileged in a decaying neoliberal system under both Hosny Mubarak and Anwar Sadat. 

Depictions of poor people varied across the eras. The most significant frame that was under investigation in this study is the accountability of poverty, and it was found that during the socialist era, as expected, poor characters were mostly seen as poor due to structural inequalities and hardships, while in the later neoliberal eras, the attention shifted to the poor character’s attitude and actions taken towards their own poverty; whether indifference or hustling to get to a better situation. The latter are damaging frames when discussing poverty, which, in most cases, is often used by structural barriers like poor education, poor access to healthcare, and, most importantly, limited access to lucrative jobs in the market that are usually reserved for those with good education and connections, in Egypt and elsewhere. 

When it came to the hero/villain dichotomy, while it was expected that films in the socialist era would have the hero frame most represented, it was actually during the following neoliberal era that saw the highest percentage of depiction of heroes. This could be attributed to the fact that while films under Sadat and Mubarak depicted poor characters as undeserving of state support, they still attached heroic Daly, 75 

features to them in what can be inferred as an emphasis on the individuality of poverty and that it is not an issue that the state is accountable for. 

Poor characters were depicted to be mostly dishonest in all eras under Sadat, where an overwhelming majority of characters were depicted to be honest. This contradicts the assumption that such positive values of honesty would feature much less during Sadat’s era than the previous era of Nasser, and could be attributed to the small sample size, and a bigger sample size could be more revealing in studying this particular frame. 

Egyptian cinema is a trendsetter in a region with limited cinematic production, and is thus an influential media force in shaping public opinion and perception of societal segments not just in Egypt but throughout the region. The main limitation of this study had been the relatively small sample size and the limited availability of literature in this line of research. Nonetheless, the researcher believes the study to be an important starting point for further research into representation and depiction of underprivileged communities in particular. As outlined and detailed in this study and many others, media framing of communities is defining of their living experiences, public attitude towards them, and even public policies that shape their opportunities and abilities to escape or better their situations. Hence, such frames need to be scrutinized and investigated for their oversized influence in impacting the lives and future of millions of people. Areas for further research include expanding the scope of this study to include other eras preceding or following the eras under investigation in this study (i.e. depictions of poor in cinema under King Farouk or under Mohamed Morsi or Abdelfattah Sisi’s regimes) the impact of these frames of audiences by method of surveying and experimenting to conclude on how audiences receive, recognize, and apply these frames in their approach to how they view poverty and poor people. An experiment where audiences are exposed to these frames in a controlled environment is potentially a fruitful area to study the immediate impact of these frames on audiences Another area for potential exploration is to examine poverty-related public policies during different political eras in Egypt to examine if there are correlations between state policies and people’s perception of poverty and poor people. question again inside every branch.

and scope. Never replace relevant rows with ellipses, examples or instructions to
continue the list. If all rows cannot fit, prioritize rows useful to the question
and explicitly mark omissions. A partial, restricted or truncated list is not the
complete candidate set. Missing fields are unknown. Keep relevant discoveries even
if they answer a different part of the original question.

do not copy their facts into your own note. Retain useful unvisited links even

## Abstract

Six years before the Egyptian revolution of January 2011, many young Egyptians had resorted to blogging as a means of self-expression and literary creativity. This resulted in the emergence of a new literary genre: the autofictional blog. Such blogs are explored here as forms of digital literature, combining literary analysis and interviews with the authors. The blogs analysed give readers a glimpse into the daily lives, feelings and aspirations of the Egyptian youth who have pushed the country towards a cultural and political revolution. The narratives are also indicative of significant aesthetic and political developments taking place in Arabic literature and culture.

[Ali Hussein Mohamed](https://independent.academia.edu/AliHusseinMohamed1)

Journal of Arab & Muslim Media Research, 2012

In authoritarian-ruled Arab societies, new media, exemplified by the Internet, are perceived as the harbinger of democracy. In interviews conducted in Egypt in 2009, I asked bloggers, human rights activists and journalists about their motivations for blogging, the nature of the relationship between blogging and traditional media practitioners and the challenges that hinder the efficacy of blogging as a social and political force. It seems clear that Egyptian blogs have been used to criticize the political order and mobilize public opinion against the regime. Moreover, the Internet and blogs are helping to transform traditional journalism, making it less susceptible to conservativism and state manipulation, enhancing political activism and expanding the reach of the public sphere.

Much has been written about the role the internet played during the Arab uprisings of 2011, with particular attention paid to social media, whether Facebook, Twitter or blogging, and the extent to which it contributed to organising the mass protests. Another recurring theme of the analysis of the uprisings was the role played by women, with Western media in particular emphasising their contributions and debating whether this marked a pronounced increase in women’s agency. My article seeks to respond to these issues through an analysis of two Egyptian women’s blogs. Instead of contributing to the well-known debate about the internet’s capabilities for facilitating action, I examine how blogs observe resistance, exploring this through notions of digital testimony and autobiography. I then consider the issue of solidarity and whether this is gendered, which is an important issue to consider in light of the focus placed on women’s roles during the protests. Ultimately I aim to demonstrate that these Egyptian women’s blogs offer us new and productive ways of thinking about the role the internet played during the Arab uprisings and the autobiographical act, leading us to acknowledge the complexities of both solidarity and articulations of selfhood.

The thesis analyses how blogging in the Arabic blogosphere conditions political authorship in exile and how new digital media technologies create novel forms of presence at a distance. This purpose is fulfilled by an in-depth analysis of the works by Yemeni blogger Afrah Nasser. The thesis relies on media theory in relation to the blog as a medium and the sociological concept of “connected migrant” to understand the literary genre of exile literature in the context of the blogosphere. The corpus under investigation in this thesis consists of two blogs created by Nasser, the first located on afrahnasser.blogspot.com and the second blog is al- Dimuqratiyya kalima murra (Democracy is a bitter word). The analysis is based on selected posts from both of Nasser’s blogs, which were published during the time of the 15th of January 2011 to the 1st of May 2015. Being uprooted, a central theme in 20th century writing, is no longer the same experience as digital technologies make global communication possible on a much larger scale and available to more people. The spatial disruption inherent in migration is today accompanied by instant ICT-mediated communication with the homeland. In Nasser's authorship this is abundantly present, as she often returns to the immediate conversations with her friends and family in Yemen, often taking place on a daily basis, as grounds for her exile writing. This, however, does not erase some of the conventional characteristics of exile literature, for example expressing a longing for returning to the homeland and frustration with the predicaments of exile. The main difference between 20th century exile authorship and Nasser’s blog authorship is a higher degree of presence and connectivity afforded by the blog as a medium.
